Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible, kept closer to the author’s own Bible where his argument rests on its wording; capitals for God in quotations (He, His) follow the BSB. “You+” marks every plural “you” (the older “ye”); a plain “you” is singular or general.

To the Reader

CHRISTIAN READER:

There are two things that I have always looked on as difficult. The one is to make the wicked sad. They do not lack cause for sadness: they are “taken captive” by Satan1. This is all that is gained by fighting on the devil’s side. He does not make his soldiers captains, but captives. He leads them as prisoners before him, and at last he will give them damnable pay. Yet sinners are so blinded by “the god of this age”2 that they cannot see the chains they are held in, but kiss their fetters and go laughing to hell. The other puzzling difficulty is to make the godly joyful. They have enough to rock their troubled hearts quiet, and may find strength “in the LORD their God”; yet like the peevish child they push away the breast and refuse to be comforted. Amnon, though a king’s son, was lean3. This dejection in the godly arises from a double spring: either their inward comforts are darkened, or their outward comforts are disturbed. To cure both these troubles I have put out this piece that follows, hoping that by the blessing of God it will buoy up their despondent hearts and make them look with a more pleasant face. I would prescribe them to take a little of this cordial now and then. When the prophet Elijah’s spirits were ready to faint under the juniper tree, the angel set before him a cake and a jar of water, and when he had eaten he was cheered, and went in the strength of that food until he came to Horeb, the mountain of God4. I think this text, like that sweet meal, may greatly strengthen and fortify the saints in their journey to heaven, and may be like a sacred feather to drop the golden oil of consolation into their hearts: “All things work together for good to those who love God.” To know that nothing will hurt the godly is a matter of comfort5; but to be assured that all things that happen will cooperate for their good, that their crosses will be turned into blessings, that the bloody showers of affliction will water the withering root of their grace and make it flourish more: here is what may fill their hearts with joy until they run over. It will be no small revival to me if these labors of mine prove helpful to anyone. When St. Paul’s prison would not allow him the liberty of a pulpit, he wrote some epistles, and the church of God has reaped their benefit in the ages since. Now that I am for the present taken off from my public work of preaching, I will be glad if I may be useful by writing, and while I myself am dead in a civil sense, I may make others alive in a spiritual sense. This is the prayer of him who is

Your friend, in all true affection and devotion,

THOMAS WATSON.

1. 2 Tim 2:25.

2. 2 Cor 4:4.

3. 2 Sam 13:4.

4. 1 Kgs 19:8.

5. Ps 91:10.

A Divine Cordial

Chapter I

The Preface, or Introduction.

Rom 8:28. We know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to His purpose.

If the whole Scripture is the feast of the soul (as St. Ambrose says), then this chapter may be a dish at this feast, which with its sweet variety may greatly refresh and enliven the hearts of God’s people. In the verses before, the apostle had been wading through the great doctrines of justification and adoption, mysteries so hard and so deep that without the help and guidance of the Spirit he might soon have waded out of his depth. In this verse the apostle touches that pleasant string of consolation: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God.” Every word is weighty, so I will gather up every filing of this gold, that nothing may be lost.

In the text there are three general branches. 1. A glorious privilege: All things work for good. 2. The persons who have a share in this privilege, and they are described in two ways: 1. they are lovers of God; 2. they are called. 3. The origin and spring of this effectual calling, set down in these words, κατὰ πρόθεσιν, according to His purpose. I will treat all these in order, and I begin with the first.

1. The glorious privilege, in which there are two things to consider: 1. The certainty of the privilege, ὄιδαμὲν, We know. 2. The excellence of the privilege, παντα συνεργει εἰς τὸ ἀγαθὸν, All things work together for good.

(1.) The certainty of the privilege: We know. It is not a matter hanging in doubt. The apostle does not say, We hope, or, We guess; it is like an article in our creed: We know all things work for good.

From this observe that the truths of the gospel6 are evident and infallible.

A Christian may come not only to a loose opinion but to a certainty about what he holds. As the axioms in logic and the aphorisms in medicine are demonstrated to reason, so the truths in religion are demonstrated to faith. We know, says the apostle. Though a Christian does not have a perfect knowledge of the mysteries of the gospel, yet he has a certain knowledge. “We see but a dim reflection as in a mirror”7 (1 Cor 13:12); so we do not have perfection of knowledge. But we behold “with unveiled faces”8 (2 Cor 3:18); so we have a certainty. The Spirit of God imprints heavenly truths on the heart as with the point of a diamond. A Christian may know infallibly that there is an evil in sin and a beauty in holiness. He may know that he is in the state of grace: “We know that we have passed from death to life” (1 John 3:14). He may know that he will go to heaven: “We know that if the earthly tent we live in is dismantled, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands” (2 Cor 5:1). The Lord does not leave his people in uncertainty in matters of salvation. The apostle comes in the text with his Probatum est [It is proved]: We know. We have arrived at a πεποίθησις, or holy confidence; we have both the Spirit of God and our own experience setting a seal to it.

Let us not rest in skepticism,9 but labor to come to a certainty in the things of religion. As that martyr woman said, “I cannot dispute for Christ, but I can burn for Christ.” God knows whether we may be called out to be witnesses to his truth, so it concerns us to be well grounded and confirmed in it. If we are doubtful Christians, we will be wavering Christians. Where does apostasy come from, but from unbelief? Men first question the truth, and then fall from the truth. O beg the Spirit of God not only to anoint you+, but to seal you+ (2 Cor 1:22).

Chapter II

Containing the Great Proposition.

2. I pass to the second, the excellence of the privilege: All things work together for good. This is a Jacob’s staff in the hand of faith, with which we may walk cheerfully to the mountain of God. What will satisfy or content us, if this will not? All things work together for good. This word συνεργεῖ, work together, is a medical expression. Several poisonous ingredients put together, when they are compounded by the skill of the apothecary, make a sovereign medicine and work together for the good of the patient10. So all God’s providences, being divinely tempered and sanctified, work together for the best for the saints. He who loves God and is called according to His purpose may say to his soul, “Take it easy,” for “you have plenty of good things laid up”: everything in the world will be for your good. This is a Christian’s cordial, which may bring the color back into his face and make him like Jonathan, who tasted the honey at the end of the staff, “and his eyes brightened” (1 Sam 14:27). Why should a Christian disembowel himself? Why should he kill himself with worry, when all things will sweetly agree, yes, conspire together, for his good? The sum of the text is this:

Doctrine. That all the various dealings of God with his children,11 by a special providence, turn to their good12.

Ps 25:10: “All the LORD’s paths are mercy to those who keep His covenant.” If every path has mercy in it, then it works for good.

(1.) What things work for good to the godly.

(2.) Why all things work for good to the godly.

(1.) What are the things that work for good to the elect?

  1. The best things.
  2. The worst things.13
