Chapter III

Showing that the best things work for good to the godly.

1. The best things work for good to the godly. There are eight of these.

The Attributes of God

1. God’s attributes work for good, these three in particular.

(1.) God’s power works for good. It is a glorious power (Col 1:11), and it is pledged for the good of the elect. Out of this strong comes sweetness14. The power of God works for good in four ways:

  1. In supporting us in misery.
  2. In supplying our needs.
  3. In subduing our corruptions.
  4. In conquering our enemies.

God’s power works for good:

[1.] In supporting us in misery: “Underneath are the everlasting arms” (Deut 33:27). What upheld Daniel in the lions’ den? What upheld Jonah in the whale’s belly, or the three young men in the furnace? Only the power of God. Is it not strange to see a bruised reed grow and flourish? How is a weak Christian able not only to endure affliction, but to rejoice in it? He is upheld by the arms of the Almighty: “My power is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor 12:9).

[2.] In supplying our needs. God creates comforts when means fail. He who brought food to the prophet Elijah by the ravens, against their nature, will bring food to his people. God can keep the oil in the jug from running dry (1 Kgs 17:14). The Lord made the sun on Ahaz’s dial go ten degrees backward. So when our outward comforts are declining, and it is almost sunset, God often brings a revival, and brings the sun many degrees backward.

[3.] In subduing our corruptions: “He will subdue our iniquities” (Mic 7:19). The Hebrew word is יכבוש, He will put them under the yoke. Is your sin strong? God is powerful; he will break the head of this Leviathan. Is your heart hard? God will dissolve that stone in Christ’s blood: “God has made my heart soft” (Job 23:16). When we say with Jehoshaphat, “We are powerless before this vast army,” the Lord goes up with us and helps us fight our battles. He strikes off the heads of those Goliath lusts that are too strong for us.

[4.] In conquering our enemies. He tarnishes the pride and breaks the confidence of adversaries15: “You will break them with an iron scepter” (Ps 2:9). There is rage in the enemy and malice in the devil, but power in God. How easily he can scatter all the forces of the wicked! “It is nothing for You, LORD, to help” (2 Chr 14:11). God’s power is on his church’s side: “Blessed are you, O Israel! … a people saved by the LORD! He is the shield that protects you, the sword in which you boast” (Deut 33:29).

(2.) The wisdom of God works for good. God’s wisdom is our oracle to instruct us. As he is the Mighty God, so he is the Counselor (Isa 9:6). We are often in the dark, and in tangled and doubtful matters we do not know which way to take. Here God comes in with light: “I will guide you with My eye” (Ps 32:8). Eye (עיני) is put there for God’s wisdom. How is it that the saints can see further than the most sharp-sighted statesmen? They foresee danger and take cover; they see Satan’s sophistries. This is οὐρανόθεν [from heaven]: God’s wisdom is the pillar of fire to go before them and guide them.

(3.) The goodness of God works for good, in two ways. 1. God’s goodness is a means to make us good: “God’s goodness leads you to repentance” (Rom 2:4). The goodness of God is a spiritual sunbeam to melt the heart into tears. “Oh,” says the soul, “has God been so good to me? Has he reprieved me from hell so long, and should I grieve his Spirit any more? Should I sin against goodness?” 2. The goodness of God works for good as it ushers in all our blessings. The daily favors we receive are the silver streams that flow from the fountain of God’s goodness. This divine attribute of goodness brings in two sorts of blessings. 1. Common blessings. All share in these, the bad as well as the good. This sweet dew falls on the thistle as well as the rose (Ps 33:5). 2. Crowning blessings. Only the godly share in these: “who crowns us with loving devotion” (Ps 103:4). So the blessed attributes of God work for good to the saints.

The Promises of God

2. The promises of God work for good. The promises are Dei Chirographum (as Augustine calls them), a bond in God’s own hand. Is it not good to have security? The promises are the breasts of the gospel, and is not the breast for the good of the infant? They are called “precious … promises” (2 Pet 1:4). They are like aqua vitae [strong spirits] to a soul that is ready to faint. Cardan says that every precious stone has some power hidden in it. The promises are full of power, and especially in four cases.

(1.) Are we under the guilt of sin? There is a promise: “The LORD, the LORD God, is merciful and gracious,” and so on (Exod 34:6). Here God puts on, as it were, his glorious embroidery and holds out the golden scepter, to encourage poor trembling sinners to come to him. The LORD … merciful. God is more willing to pardon than to punish. Mercy multiplies more in him than sin does in us. Mercy is his nature. The bee naturally gives honey; it stings only when it is provoked. “But,” says the guilty sinner, “I cannot deserve mercy.” But he is gracious. He shows mercy not because we deserve mercy, but because He delights in mercy. “But what is that to me? Perhaps my name is not in the pardon.” He keeps mercy for thousands. The treasury of mercy is not exhausted. God has treasures laid by, and why may you not come in for a child’s share? This promise is like a bezoar stone.

(2.) Are we under the defilement of sin? There is a promise working for good: “I will heal their backsliding” (Hos 14:4). God will bestow not only mercy but grace. And he has made a promise of sending his Spirit (Isa 44:3). For its sanctifying nature, the Spirit is compared in Scripture sometimes to water, which cleanses the vessel; sometimes to the wind, which is the fan to winnow and purify the air; sometimes to fire, which refines metals. So the Spirit of God will cleanse and consecrate the soul, making it a partaker of the divine nature.

(3.) Are we in great dangers? There is a promise that works for our good: “I will be with him in trouble” (Ps 91:15). God does not bring his people into troubles and leave them there; he will stand by them, and hold their head and heart when they are fainting. And there is another promise: “He is their strength in time of trouble” (Ps 37:39). “Oh,” says the soul, “I will faint in the day of trial.” But God will be the strength of our heart; he will join his forces with us. Either he will make his hand lighter, or our faith stronger.

(4.) Do we fear outward need? There is a promise: “Those who seek the LORD lack no good thing” (Ps 34:10). If it is good for us, we will have it; if it is not good for us, then not having it is good. “He will bless your bread and your water” (Exod 23:25). This blessing falls like the honeydew on the leaf; it sweetens the little we possess. Let me go without the venison, so long as I may have the blessing. Question. “But I fear I will not get a living?” Answer. Read carefully that scripture, Ps 37:25: “I once was young and now am old, yet never have I seen the righteous abandoned or their children begging for bread.” How must we understand this? 1. David speaks it as his own observation. He never saw such an eclipse; he never saw a godly man brought so low that he did not have a bite of bread to put in his mouth. 2. David never saw the righteous and their children in want. Though the Lord might test godly parents for a while by need, yet not their children too: the children of the godly will be provided for. 3. David never saw the righteous begging bread and abandoned. Though he might be brought into great straits, yet he is not abandoned. He is still an heir of heaven, and God loves him. So in all these cases the promises work for good.

How do the promises work for good?16

[1.] They are food for faith, and what strengthens faith works for good. The promises are the breast milk of faith; faith sucks nourishment from them, as the child does by drawing on the breast. Jacob was “in great fear and distress” (Gen 32:7); his spirits were ready to faint. Now he goes to the promise (verse 12): “But You have said, ‘I will surely do you good.’ ” This promise was his food. He got so much strength by sucking on this promise that he was able to wrestle with the Lord in prayer all night, and would not let him go until he had blessed him.

[2.] The promises are springs of joy. There is more in the promise to comfort than in the world to perplex. Ursinus was comforted by the promise in John 10:29: “No one can snatch them out of My Father’s hand.” The promises are cordials in a fainting fit: “If Your law had not been my delight, then I would have perished in my affliction” (Ps 119:92). The promises are like the cork on the net, to keep the heart from sinking in the deep waters of distress.

The Mercies of God

3. The mercies of God work for good to the godly.

(1.) Temporal mercies, such as health and prosperity. Mercy works most kindly on a noble spirit.

[1.] The mercies of God humble: “Then King David went in, sat before the LORD, and said, ‘Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?’ ” (2 Sam 7:18). Lord, where does such honor conferred on me come from, that I should be king? That I who followed the sheep should go in and out before your people? So a gracious heart says, Lord, what am I, that it should be better with me than with others? That I should drink of the fruit of the vine, when others drink not only a cup of wormwood but a cup of blood? What am I, that I should have those mercies that others lack, who are better than I? Lord, how is it that, in spite of all my unworthiness, a fresh tide of mercy comes in every day? The mercies of God make a sinner proud, but a saint humble.

[2.] The mercies of God have a melting influence on the soul; they dissolve it in love to God17. God’s judgments make us fear him; his mercies make us love him. How Saul was worked on by kindness! David had him at an advantage, and might have cut off not only the edge of his robe but his head; yet he spared his life. This kindness melted Saul’s heart: “Is that your voice, David my son?” Then Saul wept aloud (1 Sam 24:16). Such a melting influence God’s mercy has: it makes the eyes drop tears of love.

[3.] The mercies of God make the heart fruitful. When you spend more on a field, it bears a better crop. A gracious soul honors the LORD with his wealth. He does not do with his mercies as Israel did with their jewels and earrings, make a golden calf; but as Solomon did with the money brought into the treasury, he builds a temple for the Lord. The golden showers of mercy cause fruitfulness.

[4.] The mercies of God make the heart thankful: Quid retribuam Domino? “How can I repay the LORD for all His goodness to me? I will take the cup of salvation” (Ps 116:12, 13). David alludes to the people of Israel, who at their peace offerings used to take a cup in their hands and give thanks to God for deliverances. Every mercy is an alms of free grace, and this enlarges the soul in gratitude. A good Christian is not a grave to bury God’s mercies, but a temple to sing his praise. If every bird in its kind (as Ambrose says) chirps out thankfulness to its Maker, much more will a noble-hearted Christian, whose life is enriched and perfumed with mercy.

[5.] The mercies of God enliven us. As they are lodestones to love, so they are whetstones to obedience: “I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living” (Ps 116:9). He who looks back over his blessings regards himself as a person bound to God. He argues from the sweetness of mercy to the swiftness of duty; he spends and is spent for Christ; he dedicates his τὸ ζῆν [life] to God. Among the Romans, when one man had redeemed another, the redeemed man was to serve him ever afterward. A soul surrounded with mercy is zealously active in God’s service.

[6.] The mercies of God work compassion toward others. A Christian is a temporal savior. He feeds the hungry, clothes the naked, and visits the widow and orphan in their distress. The backs and bellies of the poor are the furrows where he sows the golden seeds of his charity: “It is well with the man who is generous and lends freely” (Ps 112:5). Charity drops from him freely, as myrrh from the tree. So to the godly the mercies of God work for good; they are wings to lift them up to heaven.

(2.) Spiritual mercies work for good: the blessed ordinances.

[1.] The word preached works for good. It is a fragrance that brings life; it is verbum cum unctione [a word with anointing]; it is a soul-transforming word. It shapes the heart into Christ’s likeness. It is the breeder of assurance: “Our gospel came to you+ not only in word, but also in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with great assurance” (1 Thess 1:5). It is vehiculum salutis, the chariot of salvation.

[2.] Prayer works for good18. Prayer is the bellows of the affections; it blows up holy desires and the fervor of the soul. Prayer has power with God: “Command Me” (Isa 45:11). It is a key that unlocks the treasury of God’s tender mercies. Prayer keeps the heart open to God and shut to sin; it cools the feverish heats and swellings of lust. It was Luther’s counsel to a friend, when he felt a temptation begin to rise, to turn to prayer. Prayer is bombarda Christianorum19, the Christians’ gun, which they fire against their enemies. Prayer is the pancreston, the sovereign medicine of the soul. Prayer sanctifies every mercy (1 Tim 4:5). It drives away sorrow: by venting the grief it eases the heart. When Hannah had prayed, she “went on her way … and her face was no longer downcast” (1 Sam 1:18). And if prayer has these rare effects, then it works for good.

[3.] The Lord’s Supper works for good. It is an emblem of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:9), and a pledge of the communion we will have with Christ in glory. It is a feast of choice food. It gives us bread from heaven, such as not only preserves life but prevents death. It has glorious effects in the hearts of the godly: it enlivens their affections, strengthens their graces, mortifies their corruptions, revives their hopes, and increases their joy. Luther says, “It is as great a work to comfort a downcast soul as to raise the dead to life.” Yet this may be done, and sometimes is done, to the souls of the godly in the blessed Supper. The sacrament has a special excellence above the word preached. In the word there is the breath of God, in the sacrament the blood of God. In the word we hear his voice, in the sacrament we have his kiss. The word comes out of God’s mouth, the sacrament out of his side.

The Graces of the Spirit

4. The graces of the Spirit work for good. Grace is to the soul as light to the eye, as health to the body. Grace does for the soul what a virtuous wife does for her husband: “She brings him good … all the days of her life” (Prov 31:12). How incomparably useful the graces are! Faith and fear go hand in hand. Faith keeps the heart cheerful; fear keeps the heart serious. Faith keeps the heart from sinking in despair; fear keeps it from floating in presumption. All the graces show themselves in their beauty: hope is the helmet (1 Thess 5:8), meekness the ornament (1 Pet 3:4), love the bond of perfection (Col 3:14). The saints’ graces are weapons to defend them, wings to lift them, jewels to enrich them, spices to perfume them, stars to adorn them20, and cordials to refresh them. And does not all this work for good? The graces are our evidences for heaven; is it not good to have our evidences ready at the hour of death?

The Created Things of God

5. The created things of God work for good to the godly. 1. Inanimate created things: “From the heavens the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera” (Judg 5:20). The stars, gathered like the host of God in battle array, raised terrible storms by their influences, and as it were conspired the ruin of Sisera and his army. 2. Animate created things. The angels, those noble citizens and princes of heaven, work for the good of the saints21. The good angels are ready to do every office of love for the people of God: “Are not all the angels ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation?” (Heb 1:14). Some of the Fathers are of the opinion that every believer has his own guardian angel. It needs no hot debate; it may be enough for us to know that the whole hierarchy of angels is employed for the good of the saints. The good angels do service to the saints:

(1.) In life. The angel comforted the virgin Mary (Luke 1:28). The angel shut the mouths of the lions so that they could not hurt Daniel (Dan 6:22). A Christian has an invisible guard about him, the keeping and guardianship of angels: “For He will command His angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways” (Ps 91:11). The angels are part of the saints’ bodyguard, yes, the chief of the angels: “Are not all the angels ministering spirits?” The highest angels take care of the lowest saints.

(2.) At death. The angels are about the saints’ sickbeds to comfort them. As God comforts by his Spirit, so he comforts by his angels. Christ in his agony was strengthened by an angel (Luke 22:43), and so are believers in the agony of death. And when the saints breathe their last, their souls are carried up to heaven by an escort of angels (Luke 16:22).

(3.) At the day of judgment. 1. The angels will open the saints’ graves, dig away the earth from their bodies, and lead them into the presence of Christ, when they will be made like his glorious body: “And He will send out His angels … and they will gather His elect from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other” (Matt 24:31). 2. At the day of judgment the angels will rid the godly of all their enemies. Here the saints are plagued with enemies: “Those who repay my good with evil attack me for pursuing the good” (Ps 38:20). Well, the angels will shortly give God’s people their discharge and set them free from all their enemies: “The weeds are the sons of the evil one … The harvest is the end of the age, and the harvesters are angels. As the weeds are collected and burned in the fire, so will it be at the end of the age. The Son of Man will send out His angels, and they will weed out of His kingdom every cause of sin and all who practice lawlessness. And they will throw them into the fiery furnace” (Matt 13:38). At the day of judgment the angels of God will take the wicked, who are the weeds, bundle them up, and throw them into the furnace of hell, and then the godly will not be troubled with enemies any more. So the good angels work for good. See here the honor and dignity of a believer. He has God’s name written on him (Rev 3:12), the Holy Spirit dwelling in him (2 Tim 1:14), and a guard of angels attending him.

Insuper nostro lateri ministros, caelitus addis. [Moreover, from heaven you set ministering spirits at our side.]

The Communion of Saints

6. The communion of saints works for good: συνεργοὶ ἐσμὲν, “we are fellow workers with you+ for your+ joy” (2 Cor 1:24). One Christian talking with another is a means to strengthen him, as the stones in an arch help to strengthen one another. One Christian, by sharing his experiences, warms and enlivens another: “Let us … spur one another on to love and good deeds” (Heb 10:24). How grace flourishes by holy conversation! A Christian, by good talk, drops such oil on another as makes the lamp of his faith burn brighter.

Christ’s Intercession

7. Christ’s intercession works for good. Christ is in heaven like Aaron with his golden plate on his forehead and his precious incense, and he prays for all believers as he did for the apostles: “I am not asking on behalf of them alone, but also on behalf of those who will believe in Me” (John 17:20). When a Christian is weak and can hardly pray for himself, Jesus Christ is praying for him. And he prays for three things. 1. That the saints may be kept from sin (verse 15): “that You keep them from evil.” We live in the world as in a plague house; Christ prays that his saints may not be infected with the contagious evil of the times. 2. For his people’s progress in holiness (verse 17): “Sanctify them.” Let them have constant supplies of the Spirit, and be anointed “with fresh oil.” 3. For their glorification (verse 24): “Father, I want those You have given Me to be with Me where I am.” Christ is not content until the saints are in his arms. This prayer that he made on earth is the copy and pattern of his prayer in heaven. What a comfort this is: when Satan is tempting, Christ is praying! This works for good.

Christ’s prayer takes away the sins of our prayers. A child (says St. Ambrose) who wants to present his father with a posy goes into the garden and gathers some flowers and some weeds together. But when he comes to his mother, she picks out the weeds and binds up the flowers, and so it is presented to the father. So when we have offered up our prayers, Christ comes and picks away the weeds, the sin of our prayer, and presents nothing but flowers to his Father, which are a sweet-smelling fragrance.

The Saints’ Prayers

8. The joint stock of the saints’ prayers works for good to the godly. The saints pray for all the members of the mystical body, and their prayers prevail much22. 1. They prevail for recovery from sickness: “The prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up” (Jas 5:15). 2. For victory over enemies: “Lift up a prayer for the remnant that still survives” (Isa 37:4); “Then the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians” (verse 36). 3. For deliverance out of prison: “The church was fervently praying to God for him” (Acts 12:5); “Suddenly an angel of the Lord appeared and a light shone in the cell. He tapped Peter on the side and woke him up … And the chains fell off his wrists” (verse 7). The angel fetched Peter out of prison, but it was prayer that fetched the angel. 4. For forgiveness of sin: “My servant Job will pray for you+, for I will accept his prayer” (Job 42:8). So the prayers of the saints work for good to the mystical body. And this is no small privilege for a child of God, that he has a constant trade of prayer carried on for him. When he comes into any town or city, he may say, I have some prayer here; indeed, all the world over I have a stock of prayer going for me. When I am out of sorts and out of tune, others are praying for me who are alert and lively. So the best things work for good to the people of God.

14. Judg 14:14.

15. οὐδὲν ἰσχυρότερον τοῦ τῆς ἄνωθεν συμμαχίας ἀπολαύοντος. [Nothing is stronger than the one who enjoys the alliance from above.] Chrysostom

16. Question. Answer. 1.

17. Διὰ τοῦτο πολλὰς ἐις ἡμᾶς ἐυεργεσίας κατατίθεται ὁ θεὸς ἵνα ἡμᾶς ἐφελκύσηται. [For this reason God lays up many benefits for us, that he may draw us to himself.] Chrysost.

18. παντὸς ἀγαθοῦ κεφάλαιον ἐστιν ἡ προσευχὴ. [Prayer is the sum of every good thing.] Chr. orat. de prec.

19. Luther.

20. ψυχὴ λαμπροτέρα γίνεται τὴν δεξαμένη χάριν. [The soul that has received grace becomes brighter.]

21. Domestici Dei, caeli cives, principes paradisi. [Members of God’s household, citizens of heaven, princes of paradise.] Bernard

22. Αἱ ψυχαὶ διὰ τῶν ἁγίων προσευχῶν ἁρμόζονται καὶ δρόμον τῆς ἐυσεβείας τρέχουσιν ἐυχερῶς. [Through the prayers of the saints, souls are set in order and run the course of godliness with ease.]

Chapter IV

Showing that the worst things work for good to the godly.

2. The worst things work for good to the godly23. Do not mistake me. I do not say that they are good in their own nature24, for they are a fruit of the curse. But though they are naturally evil, yet they are morally good, as the wise, overruling hand of God disposes and sanctifies them. Take the elements: though they are of contrary qualities, yet God has so blended them that they all work in a harmonious way for the good of the universe. Or take a watch: the wheels seem to move contrary to one another, but all carry on the motion of the watch and help to make the alarm strike. So things that seem to move against the godly yet work for their good by the wonderful providence of God. Among these κάκιστα, worst things, there are four sad evils that work for good to those who love God.

SECTION I. Showing that the evil of affliction works for good to the godly.

1. The evil of affliction works for good. There are two heart-quieting considerations in all the afflictions that befall us.

(1.) The first is that God has a special hand in them: “The Almighty has afflicted me” (Ruth 1:21). Instruments can no more stir until God gives them a commission than the axe can cut by itself without a hand. Job saw God in his affliction. So, as Augustine observes, he does not say, “The LORD gave, and the devil took away”25, but, “The LORD has taken away.” Whoever brings an affliction to us, it is God who sends it.

(2.) The second heart-quieting consideration is that afflictions work for good. Jer 24:5: “Like these good figs, so I regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans for their good.” Judah’s captivity in Babylon was לטובה, for their good. Ps 119:71: “It was good for me to be afflicted”26. This text, like the tree Moses threw into the bitter waters, may make the bitter waters of affliction sweet and wholesome to drink. Afflictions to the godly are medicinal. Out of the most poisonous drug God draws our salvation. Afflictions are as needful as ordinances (1 Pet 1:6). No vessel can be made of gold without fire; so it is impossible that we should be made vessels of honor unless we are melted and refined in the furnace of affliction. Ps 25:10: “All the LORD’s paths are mercy”: his bloody paths are mercy. As the painter mixes bright colors with dark shadows, so the wise God mixes mercy with judgment. The afflicting providences that seem to be harmful are beneficial. Let us take some instances in Scripture. Joseph’s brothers threw him into a pit, afterward they sold him, then he was cast into prison; yet all this worked for his good. His abasement made way for his advancement: he was made the second man in the kingdom. Gen 50:20: “As for you+, what you+ intended against me for evil, God intended for good.” Jacob wrestled with the angel, and the hollow of Jacob’s thigh was put out of joint. This was sad, but God turned it to good, for there he saw God’s face, and there the Lord blessed him (Gen 32:30): “So Jacob named the place Peniel, saying, ‘Indeed, I have seen God face to face.’” Who would not be willing to have a bone out of joint, if he might have a sight of God? King Manasseh was bound in chains. It was sad to see a crown of gold changed into fetters, but it worked for his good, for “in his affliction, Manasseh sought the favor of the LORD his God and earnestly humbled himself … and the LORD received his plea” (2 Chr 33:11, 12). He owed more to his iron chain than to his gold chain: the one made him proud, the other made him humble. Job was a spectacle of misery. He lost all that he ever had; he abounded only in boils and ulcers. This was sad, but it worked for his good: his grace was more tested and improved. God gave a testimony from heaven to his integrity, and made up his loss by giving him twice as much as he ever had before (Job 42:10). Paul was struck with blindness. This was distressing, but it turned to his good. By that blindness God made way for the light of grace to shine into his soul; it was the beginning of a happy conversion (Acts 9:6).

As the hard frosts in winter bring on the flowers in the spring, and as the night ushers in the morning star, so the evils of affliction produce much good to those who love God. But we are ready to question the truth of this, and to say as Mary did to the angel, “How can this be?” So I will show you+ several ways in which affliction works for good.

[1.] Affliction works for good as it is our preacher and tutor: “Hear the rod” (Mic 6:9)27. Luther says that he could never rightly understand some of the Psalms until he was in affliction. Affliction teaches two things. 1. What sin is. In the word preached we hear what a dreadful thing sin is, that it both defiles and damns; but we fear it no more than a painted lion. So God lets affliction loose, and then we feel how bitter sin is in its fruit. A sickbed often teaches more than a sermon; we can best see the ugly face of sin in the mirror of affliction. 2. Affliction teaches us to know ourselves. In prosperity we are for the most part strangers to ourselves. God makes us know affliction so that we may know ourselves better. In a time of affliction we see corruption in our hearts that we would not believe was there. Water in the glass looks clear, but set it on the fire, and the scum boils up. In prosperity a man seems to be humble and thankful, and the water looks clear; but set this man on the fire of affliction a little, and the scum boils up: much impatience and unbelief appear. “Oh,” says a Christian, “I never thought I had such a bad heart as I now see I have. I never thought my corruptions were so strong and my graces so weak.”

[2.] Afflictions work for good as they are a means to make the heart more upright. In prosperity the heart is apt to be divided (Hos 10:2). The heart clings partly to God and partly to the world. It is like a needle between two lodestones: God draws, and the world draws. Now God takes away the world, so that the heart may cling more to him in sincerity. Corrigere, quasi cor rectum facere; correction is setting the heart right and straight. As we sometimes hold a crooked stick over the fire to straighten it, so God holds us over the fire of affliction to make us more straight and upright. Oh how good it is, when sin has bent the soul away from God, that affliction should straighten it again!

[3.] Afflictions work for good as they conform us to Christ. God’s rod is a pencil to draw Christ’s image on us more vividly. It is good that there should be a symmetry and proportion between the Head and the members. Would we be parts of Christ’s mystical body, and not be like him? His life (as Calvin says) was a series of sufferings: “a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief” (Isa 53:3). He wept; he bled. Was the Head crowned with thorns, and do we think to be crowned with roses? It is good to be like Christ, though it is by sufferings. Jesus Christ drank a bitter cup; it made him sweat drops of blood to think of it. And though it is true that he drank the poison in the cup (the wrath of God), yet there is some wormwood left in the cup, which the saints must drink. Only here is the difference between Christ’s sufferings and ours: his were to make satisfaction for sin; ours are only to correct.

[4.] Afflictions work for good to the godly as they are destructive to sin. Sin is the mother, affliction is the daughter; the daughter helps to destroy the mother. Sin is like the tree that breeds the worm, and affliction is like the worm that eats the tree. There is much corruption in the best heart, and affliction works it out by degrees, as the fire works the dross out of the gold. Isa 27:9: “the full fruit of the removal of his sin.” What if we have more of the rough file, if we have less rust? Afflictions carry away nothing but the filth of sin. Suppose a physician should say to a patient, “Your body is diseased and full of infection, which must be purged out, or you die; but I will prescribe medicine which, though it makes you deadly sick, yet will carry away the dregs of your disease and save your life.” Would this not be for the good of the patient? Afflictions are the purging pills God uses to carry away our spiritual diseases. They cure the swelling of pride, the fever of lust, the dropsy of covetousness. Do they not then work for good?

[5.] Afflictions work for good as they are a means to loosen our hearts from the world. When you dig the earth away from the root of a tree, it is to loosen the tree from the earth. So God digs away our earthly comforts to loosen our hearts from the earth28. We read of a star (Rev 8:11): “The name of the star is Wormwood.” Have we not seen this star appear? Do we not find this star Wormwood in every condition? A thorn grows up with every flower.

Surgit amari aliquid quod in ipsis floribus angat. [Something bitter rises up to pain us among the very flowers.]

God would have the world hang like a loose tooth, which does not trouble us much when it is pulled away. Is it not good to be weaned? The oldest saint needs it. Why does the Lord break the conduit pipe, but that we may go to him in whom are all our fresh springs29?

[6.] Afflictions work for good as they make way for comfort. God makes “the Valley of Achor into a gateway of hope” (Hos 2:15). Achor means trouble. God sweetens outward pain with inward peace. John 16:20: “Your+ grief will turn to joy.” Here is the water turned into wine. After a bitter pill God gives sugar. Paul had his prison songs. God’s rod has honey at the end of it. The saints in affliction have had such sweet raptures of joy that they have thought themselves on the borders of the heavenly Canaan; they have gathered grapes from thorns.

[7.] Afflictions work for good as they magnify us. Job 7:17: “What is man that You should magnify him … that You attend to him every morning?” God magnifies us by affliction in three ways. 1. In that he will stoop so low as to take notice of us, and will afflict us rather than lose us. It is an honor that God will mind dust and ashes; it magnifies us that God thinks us worthy to be struck. God’s not striking is a slighting: “Why should you+ be stricken any more?” (Isa 1:5). If you+ will go on in sin, take your+ course, sin yourselves+ into hell. 2. Afflictions magnify us as they are insignia honoris, ensigns of glory, signs of sonship. Heb 12:7: “Endure suffering as discipline; God is treating you+ as sons.” Every print of the rod is a badge of honor. 3. Afflictions really tend to magnify the saints, as they make them renowned in the world. Soldiers have never been so admired for their victories as the saints have been for their sufferings. The zeal and constancy of the martyrs in their trials have made them famous to later ages. How eminent Job was for his patience! God leaves his name on record: “You+ have heard of Job’s patience” (Jas 5:11). Job the sufferer was more renowned than Alexander the conqueror.

[8.] Afflictions work for good as they are a means to make us happy. Job 5:17: “Happy is the man whom God corrects.” What statesman or moralist ever placed happiness in the cross? Job does: “Happy is the man whom God corrects.”

Question. How do afflictions make us happy?

Answer. In that afflictions, when they are sanctified, bring us nearer to God30. The moon at the full is further from the sun; so many are further from God in the full moon of prosperity, and affliction brings them nearer to God. The lodestone of mercy does not draw us so near to God as the cords of affliction do. When Absalom set Joab’s grain on fire, Joab came running to Absalom (2 Sam 14:30). When God sets our worldly comforts on fire, then we run to him and make our peace with him. When the prodigal was pinched with need, then he returned home to his father (Luke 15:18). When the dove could find no rest for the sole of her foot, she flew to the ark; when God brings a flood of affliction on us, then we fly to the ark, Christ. So affliction makes us happy by bringing us nearer to God31. Faith can make use of the waters of affliction to swim faster to Christ.

[9.] Afflictions work for good as they put the wicked to silence. How ready they are to slander and malign the godly, saying that they serve God only for self-interest! So God will have his people endure sufferings for religion, that he may hang a padlock on the lying lips of wicked men. When the atheists of the world see that God has a people who serve him not for wages but for love, this stops their mouths. The devil accused Job of hypocrisy, of being a mercenary man whose religion was all made up of aims at gold and silver. Job 1:9, 10: “Does Job fear God for nothing? Have You not placed a hedge … around him?” and so on. “Well,” says God, “put out your hand; touch his estate.” No sooner had the devil received a commission than he fell to breaking down Job’s hedge. Yes, but Job still worships God (chapter 1:20), and professes his faith in him (chapter 13:15): “Though He slay me, I will trust in Him.” This amazed and silenced the devil himself. How it strikes a chill into wicked men when they see that the godly will iratum colere numen, keep close to God in a suffering condition, and when they lose all, will still hold fast their integrity!

[10.] Afflictions work for good as they make way for glory (2 Cor 4:17). Not that they merit glory, but they prepare for it. As plowing prepares the earth for a crop, so afflictions prepare us and make us fit for glory. The painter lays his gold on dark colors. So God first lays on the dark colors of affliction, and then he lays on the golden color of glory. The vessel is first seasoned before wine is poured into it; the vessels of mercy are first seasoned with affliction, and then the wine of glory is poured in32. So we see that afflictions are not harmful but beneficial to the saints. We should not look so much at the evil of affliction as at the good, not so much at the dark side of the cloud as at the light. The worst that God does to his children is to whip them to heaven.

SECTION II. Showing that the evil of temptation works for good to the godly.

2. The evil of temptation works for good. Satan is called ὁ πειράζων, the tempter (Matt 4:3). He is always lying in ambush: stat in procinctu Diabolus [the devil stands ready for battle]. He is continually at work with one saint or another33. The devil has his circuit, or diocese, that he walks every day. He is not yet fully cast into prison, but like a prisoner who is out on bail, he walks about to tempt the saints. This is a great trouble to a child of God, as it is a trouble to a virgin to have her chastity assaulted daily. Now concerning Satan’s temptations, there are three things to be considered:

  1. His method in tempting.
  2. The extent of his power.
  3. That these temptations work for good.

(1.) Satan’s method in tempting. Here take notice of two things.

[1.] His violence in tempting, and so he is the red dragon. He labors to storm the castle of the heart. He throws in thoughts of blasphemy; he tempts us to deny God. These are the fiery darts he shoots, by which he would inflame the passions.

[2.] His subtlety in tempting, and so he is the old serpent. There are five chief subtleties the devil uses.

1st. He observes a man’s temperament and constitution, and lays baits of temptation to suit it. As the farmer knows what grain is right for the soil, so Satan will not tempt contrary to the natural disposition and temperament. This is his strategy: he makes the wind and the tide go together. The way the natural tide of the heart runs, that way the wind of temptation blows. Though the devil cannot know men’s thoughts, yet he knows their temperament, and he lays his baits accordingly. —Omnium discutit more [he examines the ways of all]— He tempts the ambitious man with a crown, the passionate man with beauty.

2nd. Satan watches for the fittest time to tempt, as a cunning angler casts in his hook when the fish will bite best. Satan’s time of tempting is usually after an ordinance, and the reason is that then he thinks he will find us most off our guard. When we have been at solemn duties, we are apt to think all is done, and we grow slack and leave off the zeal and strictness we had before. We are just like a soldier who takes off his armor after a battle, never once dreaming of an enemy. Now Satan watches his time, and when we least suspect it, he throws in a temptation.

3rd. He makes use of near relations; the devil tempts by proxy. So he handed a temptation to Job by his wife: “Do you still retain your integrity?” (Job 2:9). A wife in the bosom may be the devil’s instrument to tempt to sin.

4th. Satan tempts to evil by those who are good; so he gives poison in a golden cup. He tempted Christ by Peter. Peter tried to dissuade him from suffering: “Master, pity yourself.” Who would have thought to find the tempter in the mouth of an apostle?

5th. Satan tempts to sin under a pretense of religion. He is most to be feared when he “masquerades as an angel of light.” He came to Christ with Scripture in his mouth: “It is written.” The devil baits his hook with religion. He tempts many a man to covetousness and extortion under a pretense of providing for his family. He tempts some to do away with themselves, so that they may live no longer to sin against God; and so he draws them into sin under a pretense of avoiding sin. These are his νοήματα, his subtle stratagems in tempting.

(2.) The extent of his power: how far Satan’s power in tempting reaches.

[1.] He can set the object before us, as he set a bar of gold before Achan.

[2.] He can poison the imagination and instill evil thoughts into the mind. As the Holy Spirit casts in good promptings, so the devil casts in bad ones. He put it into Judas’s heart to betray Christ (John 13:2).—

[3.] Satan can stir up and provoke the corruption within, and work a kind of inclination in the heart to embrace a temptation. It is true that Satan cannot force the will to consent; yet, being an earnest suitor, he may provoke to evil by his continual soliciting. So he provoked David to number the people (1 Chr 21:1).—The devil may argue us into sin by his subtle arguments.

(3.) These temptations work for good to the children of God. A tree that is shaken by the wind is more settled and rooted; so the blowing of a temptation only settles a Christian the more in grace. Temptations work for good in eight ways.

[1.] Temptation sends the soul to prayer. The more furiously Satan tempts, the more fervently the saint prays. The deer, when it is shot with the dart, runs faster to the water; when Satan shoots his fiery darts at the soul, it runs faster to the throne of grace. When Paul had the messenger of Satan to buffet him: “Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away from me” (2 Cor 12:8). Temptation is a medicine for complacency. Whatever makes us pray more works for good.

[2.] Temptation to sin is a means to keep us from committing sin. The more a child of God is tempted, the more he fights against the temptation. The more Satan tempts to blasphemy, the more a saint trembles at such thoughts and says, “Away from me, Satan!” When Joseph’s mistress tempted him to folly, the stronger her temptation was, the stronger his resistance was. The temptation the devil uses as a spur to sin, God makes a bridle to hold a Christian back from it. The more a chaste virgin is assaulted, the more she abhors the proposal.

[3.] Temptation works for good as it brings down the swelling of pride. 2 Cor 12:7: “So to keep me from becoming conceited, I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me.” The thorn in the flesh was to prick the bladder of pride34. Better is the temptation that humbles me than the duty that makes me proud. Rather than let a Christian be haughty-minded, God will let him fall into the devil’s hands for a while, to be cured of his abscess.

[4.] Temptation works for good as it is a touchstone to try what is in the heart. The word tentare [to tempt] means explorare [to search out]. The devil tempts so that he may deceive; but God allows us to be tempted to try us. 1. Temptation is a trial of our sincerity. It shows that our heart is chaste and loyal to Christ when we can look a temptation in the face and turn our back on it. 2. It is a trial of our courage. Hos 7:11: “Ephraim has become like a silly dove, without a heart.” So it may be said of many that they are without a heart: they have no heart to resist temptation. No sooner does Satan come than they yield, like a coward who gives the thief his purse as soon as the thief approaches. But he is the valiant Christian who brandishes the sword of the Spirit against Satan, and will rather die than yield. The courage of the Romans was never more seen than when they were assaulted by the Carthaginians; the valor and might of a saint is never more seen than in a pitched battle, when he is fighting with the red dragon and by the power of faith puts the devil to flight. That grace is tried gold which can stand in the fiery trial and withstand fiery darts. Fidei robur potest esse concussum, non excussum [The strength of faith may be shaken, but not shaken off]35.

[5.] Temptations work for good as God makes those who are tempted fit to comfort others in the same distress. A Christian must himself be under the buffetings of Satan before he can speak a word in due season to him who is weary. St. Paul was well versed in temptations: “We are not unaware of his schemes” (2 Cor 2:11). And he was able to acquaint others with Satan’s cursed wiles (1 Cor 10:13). A man who has ridden over a place where there are bogs and quicksands is the fittest to guide others through that dangerous way. He who has felt the claws of the roaring lion, and has lain bleeding under those wounds, is the fittest man to deal with one who is tempted. None can better uncover Satan’s tricks and stratagems than those who have been long in the fencing school of temptation.

[6.] Temptations work for good as they stir up a father’s compassion in God toward those who are tempted. The child who is sick and bruised is looked after most. When a saint lies under the bruisings of temptation, Christ prays, and God the Father pities. When Satan puts the soul into a fever, God comes with a cordial. That is what made Luther say that temptations are amplexus Christi, Christ’s embraces, because he then most sweetly reveals himself to the soul.

[7.] Temptations work for good as they make the saints long more for heaven. There they will be out of gunshot. Heaven is a place of rest; no bullets of temptation fly there. The eagle that soars aloft in the air and sits on high trees is not troubled with the stinging of the serpent. So when believers have gotten up into the highest heaven, they will not be troubled by the old serpent36. In this life, when one temptation is over, another comes. This is to make God’s people long for the time when death sounds a retreat and calls them off the field where the bullets fly so thick, to receive a victor’s crown, where not the drum or the cannon, but the harp and the viol, will always be sounding.

[8.] Temptations work for good as they engage the strength of Christ. Christ is our friend, and when we are tempted, he sets all his power to work for us37: “Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted”38. If a poor soul had to fight alone with the Goliath of hell, he would be sure to be overcome. But Jesus Christ brings in his auxiliary forces; he gives fresh supplies of grace (2 Cor 12:9). And in him ὑπερνικῶμὲν, “we are more than conquerors.” So the evil of temptation works for good.

But sometimes Satan defeats a child of God; how does this work for good39?

I grant that through the suspension of divine grace and the fury of a temptation a saint may be overcome. Yet this defeat by a temptation will work for good40. 1. By this defeat God makes way for the increase of grace. Peter was tempted to self-confidence; he presumed on his own strength. And when he would insist on standing alone, Christ let him fall. But this worked for his good. It cost him many a tear: “he went outside and wept bitterly.” And now he grew more modest. He dared not say that he loved Christ more than the other apostles. John 21:15: “Do you love Me more than these?” He dared not say so; his fall broke the neck of his pride. 2. Defeat by a temptation causes more circumspection and watchfulness in a child of God. Though Satan decoyed him into sin before, yet for the future he will be the more cautious. He will take care not to come within the lion’s chain any more. He is more shy and fearful of the occasions of sin. He never goes out without his spiritual armor, and he girds on his armor by prayer. He knows he walks on slippery ground, so he looks warily to his steps. He keeps close sentry in his soul, and when he spies the devil coming, he stands to his arms and holds up the shield of faith (Eph 6:16). This is all the hurt the devil does: when he defeats a saint by temptation, he cures him of his careless neglect, and makes him watch and pray more. When wild beasts get over the hedge and hurt the grain, a man will make his fence the stronger. So when the devil gets over the hedge by a temptation, a Christian will be sure to mend his fence; he is more fearful of sin, and more careful of duty. So being worsted by temptation works for good.

Objection. But if being defeated works for good, may this not make Christians careless whether they are overcome by temptations or not?

Response. There is a great deal of difference between falling into a temptation and running into a temptation. Falling into a temptation will work for good, not running into it. He who falls into a river may be helped and pitied, but he who recklessly plunges into it is guilty of his own death. It is madness to run into a lion’s den. He who runs himself into a temptation is like Saul, who “took his own sword and fell on it.”

From all that has been said, by way of conclusion, see how God makes a fool of the old serpent, by making his temptations turn to the good of his people. Surely if the devil knew how much benefit comes to the saints by temptation, he would stop tempting41. Luther once said that three things make a Christian: prayer, meditation, temptation. After a fever the body shoots up more in stature; after believers have been in a hot fit of temptation, they have shot up more in holiness. St. Paul on his voyage to Rome met with a contrary wind (Acts 27:4). So the wind of temptation is a wind contrary to that of the Spirit; but God makes use of this cross wind to blow the saints to heaven.

SECTION III. Showing that the evil of desertion works for good to the godly.

3. The evil of desertion works for good. The bride complains of desertion. Song 5:6: “my beloved had withdrawn himself and gone.” There is a twofold withdrawing. Either it is 1. in regard of grace, when God suspends the influence of his Spirit and withholds the lively actings of grace. If the Spirit is gone, grace freezes into chilliness and numbness. Or it is 2. a withdrawing in regard of comfort, when God withholds the sweet manifestations of his favor. He does not look with such a pleasant face, but veils his face, and seems to be quite gone from the soul.

God is just in all his withdrawings: we desert him before he deserts us42. We desert God when we leave off close communion with him; when we desert his truths and dare not appear for him; when we leave the guidance and direction of his word and follow the ignis fatuus [will-o’-the-wisp] of our own corrupt affections and passions. We usually desert God first, so we have no one to blame but ourselves.

Desertion is very sad. For as darkness follows in the air when the light is withdrawn, so when God withdraws there is darkness and sorrow in the soul. Desertion is an agony of conscience, as Alstead calls it; God holds the soul over hell. Job 6:4: “The arrows of the Almighty have pierced me; my spirit drinks in their poison.” It was a custom among the Persians in their wars (as Drusius notes) to dip their arrows in the poison of serpents to make them more deadly. So God shot the poisoned arrow of desertion into Job, and under its wounds his spirit lay bleeding. In times of desertion the people of God are apt to be dejected. They dispute against themselves and think that God has quite cast them off. So I will prescribe some comfort to the deserted soul. When the sailor has no star to guide him, yet he has light in his lantern, which is some help to him. So when the poor soul is sailing in the dark of desertion and lacks the bright morning star, I will lay down four consolations, which are like the sailor’s lantern to give some light.

(1.) None but the godly are capable of desertion. Wicked men do not know what God’s love means, nor what it is to lack it. They know what it is to lack health, friends, and trade, but not what it is to lack God’s favor. You fear that you are not God’s child because you are deserted, whereas none but the godly are deserted. The Lord cannot be said to withdraw his love from the wicked, because they never had it. Being deserted shows you to be a child of God. How could you complain that God has estranged himself, if you had not at times received smiles and love tokens from him?

(2.) There may be the seed of grace where there is not the flower of joy. The earth may lack a crop of grain, yet may have a mine of gold within. A Christian may have grace within, though the luscious fruit of joy does not grow. Ships at sea that are richly laden with jewels and spices may be in the dark and be tossed in the storm. A soul enriched with the treasures of grace may yet be in the dark of desertion, and so tossed as to think it will be cast away in the storm. David, in a comfortless state, prays, “take not Your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps 51:11). He does not pray, says Augustine, “Lord, give me your Spirit,” but, Ne tollas spiritum, “Do not take away your Spirit.” So he still had the Spirit of God remaining in him.

(3.) These desertions are only for a time. Christ may go into the withdrawing room and leave the soul for a while, but he will come again. Isa 54:8: “In a little wrath I hid My face from you for a moment, but with everlasting kindness I will have compassion on you.” When it is dead low water, the tide will come in again. Isa 57:16: “I will not always be angry; for then the spirit of man would grow weak before Me, with the breath of those I have made.” The tender mother sets her child down in anger, but she will take it up into her arms again and kiss it. God may put the soul away in anger, but he will take it up again into his dear embraces and display the banner of love over it.

(4.) These desertions work for good to the godly, and in seven ways.

[1.] Desertion works a cure on the soul. 1. It cures sinful drowsiness. We find the bride fallen on the bed of sloth: “I sleep” (Song 5:2). And at once Christ was gone (verse 6): “my beloved had withdrawn himself.” Who will speak to someone who is drowsy? 2. Desertion cures excessive love of the world. 1 John 2:15: “Do not love the world.” We may hold the world like a posy in our hand, but it must not lie too near our heart. We may use it as an inn where we stop for a meal, but it must not be our home. Perhaps these worldly things steal the heart away too much. Good men are at times sick with a surfeit and drunk with the luscious delights of prosperity. They have spotted their silver wings of grace and much defaced God’s image by rubbing it against the earth. To recover them from this, the Lord hides his face in a cloud. This eclipse has good effects: it darkens all the glory of the world and makes it disappear.

[2.] Desertion works for good as it makes the saints prize God’s countenance more than ever. Ps 63:3: “Your loving devotion is better than life.” Yet the commonness of this mercy lowers its value. When pearls grew common at Rome, they began to be slighted. God has no better way to make us value his love than by withdrawing it for a while. If the sun shone only once a year, how it would be prized! When the soul has long been benighted with desertion, oh how welcome then is the return of the Sun of Righteousness!

[3.] Desertion works for good as it is a means to make sin bitter to us. Can there be a greater misery than to have God’s displeasure? What makes hell but the hiding of God’s face? And what makes God hide his face but sin? John 20:13: “they have taken my Lord away, and I do not know where they have laid Him.” So our sins have taken away the Lord, and we do not know where he is laid. The favor of God is the best jewel: it can sweeten a prison and take the sting out of death. Oh how hateful then is the sin that robs us of our best jewel! Sin made God desert his temple (Ezek 8:6). Sin makes him appear as an enemy and dress himself in armor. This makes the soul pursue sin with a holy malice and seek to be avenged on it. The deserted soul gives sin gall and vinegar to drink, and with the spear of mortification lets out its heart’s blood.

[4.] Desertion works for good as it produces these three gracious effects.

1st. It sets the soul weeping for the loss of God. When the sun is gone, the dew falls; and when God is gone, tears drop from the eyes. How troubled Micah was when he had lost his gods! Judg 18:24: “You+ took the gods I had made … What else do I have?” So when God is gone, what else do we have? It is not the harp and the viol that can comfort when God is gone. Though it is sad to lack God’s presence, yet it is good to lament his absence.

2nd. Desertion sets the soul seeking after God. When Christ had stepped aside, the bride pursued him. She sought him “through the streets” of the city (Song 3:2). And when a non inventus [not found] was returned, she raised a hue and cry after him (verse 3): “Have you+ seen the one I love?” The deserted soul sends up whole volleys of sighs and groans. It knocks at heaven’s gate by prayer; it can have no rest until the golden beams of God’s face shine.

3rd. Desertion sets the Christian inquiring. He inquires into the cause of God’s departure: What is the accursed thing that has made God angry? Perhaps pride, perhaps a surfeit of ordinances, perhaps worldliness. Isa 57:17: “I was enraged by his sinful greed … and hid My face.” Perhaps there is some secret sin allowed. A stone in the pipe hinders the flow of water; so sin that is lived in hinders the sweet flow of God’s love. So conscience, like a bloodhound, finds out sin and overtakes it, and this Achan is stoned to death.

[5.] Desertion works for good as it gives us a sight of what Jesus Christ suffered for us. If sipping the cup is so bitter, how bitter was the cup Christ drank on the cross? He drank a cup of deadly poison, which made him cry out, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” None can feel Christ’s sufferings so deeply, none can be so fired with love for Christ, as those who have been humbled by desertion and held over the flames of hell for a time.

[6.] Desertion works for good as it prepares the saints for future comfort. The nipping frosts prepare for spring flowers. It is God’s way first to cast down and then to comfort (2 Cor 7:6). When our Savior had been fasting, then the angels came and ministered to him. When the Lord has kept his people fasting long, then he sends the Comforter and feeds them with the hidden manna. Ps 97:11: אור זרע, “Light is sown for the righteous.” The saints’ comforts may be hidden like seed underground, but the seed is ripening, and will increase and flourish into a crop.

[7.] These desertions work for good as they will make heaven the sweeter to us. Here our comforts are like the moon: at times they are at the full, at times on the wane. God shows himself to us for a while, and then retires into the withdrawing room. How this will set off heaven the more, and make it more delightful and ravishing, when we will have a constant look of love from God (1 Thess 4:17)!

So we see that desertions work for good. The Lord brings us into the deep of desertion so that he may not bring us into the deep of damnation. He puts us into a seeming hell so that he may keep us from a real hell. God is fitting us for the time when we will enjoy his smiles forever, when there will be neither clouds on his face nor sunsetting, when Christ will come and stay with his bride and kiss her with the kisses of his lips, and the bride will never again say, “My beloved has withdrawn himself.”

SECTION IV. Showing that the evil of sin works for good to the godly.

4. The evil of sin works for good: not in its own nature (for it is damnable), but as God in his infinite wisdom overrules it. This is St. Augustine’s comment on the text43. I may now say, as the apostle does in another sense, “Listen, I tell you+ a mystery” (1 Cor 15:51): sin itself works for good to the godly. Indeed, it is a matter of wonder that any honey should come out of this lion. — We may understand it in a double sense.

(1.) The sins of others work for good to the godly. It is no small trouble to a gracious heart to live among the wicked. Ps 120:5: “Woe to me that I dwell in Meshech.” Yet even this the Lord turns to good.

[1.] The sins of others work for good as they breed holy sorrow. God’s people weep for what they cannot reform. Ps 119:136: “My eyes shed streams of tears because Your law is not obeyed.” David was a mourner for the sins of the times; his heart was turned into a spring, and his eyes into rivers. Wicked men make merry with sin: “when you do evil, then you rejoice” (Jer 11:15). But the godly are weeping doves. They grieve for the oaths and blasphemies of the age; they take the sins of others and make them spears to pierce their own souls. This grieving for the sins of others is good. 1. It shows a childlike heart. It is a mark of a noble nature to feel with sorrow the injuries done to our heavenly Father. 2. It shows a Christlike heart. Mark 3:5: He looked on them with “sorrow at their hardness of heart.” 3. The Lord takes special notice of these tears; he is well pleased that we should weep when his glory suffers. It shows more grace to grieve for the sins of others than for our own. We may grieve for our own sins out of fear of hell, but to grieve for the sins of others comes from a principle of love to God. These tears drop like water from the roses; they are sweet and fragrant, and God puts them in his bottle.

[2.] The sins of others work for good to the godly as they set them praying the more against sin. If there were not such a spirit of wickedness at large, perhaps there would not be such a spirit of prayer. Crying sins cause crying prayers. The people of God pray against the iniquity of the times, that God would put a check on sin and put sin to shame. If they cannot pray down sin, they pray against it; and God takes this kindly. These prayers will be both recorded and rewarded. Though we do not prevail in prayer, we will not lose our prayers. Ps 35:13: “my prayer returned to my own bosom.”

[3.] The sins of others work for good as they make us the more in love with grace. The sins of others are a foil to set off the luster of grace the more. One contrary sets off another: deformity sets off beauty. The sins of the wicked greatly disfigure them. Pride is a disfiguring sin: an ambitious man is only a bladder the devil has blown up. Now seeing another’s pride makes us the more in love with humility. Malice is a disfiguring sin; it is the devil’s picture. The more of this we see in others, the more we fall in love with meekness and kindness. Drunkenness is a disfiguring sin. Like Circe’s cup, it turns men into beasts; it robs them of the use of reason. The more intemperate we see others to be, the more we fall in love with sobriety. The black face of sin sets off the beauty of holiness so much the more.

[4.] The sins of others work for good as they work in us a stronger opposition to sin. Ps 119:126: “they have broken Your law. Therefore I love Your law.” David would never have loved God’s law so much if the wicked had not set themselves so much against it. The more violent others are against the truth, the more valiant the saints are for it. Living fish swim against the stream; the more the tide of sin comes in, the more the godly swim against it. The wickedness of the times stirs up holy anger in the saints: the anger that is against sin is without sin. The sins of others are like a whetstone to set a sharper edge on us; they whet our zeal and indignation against sin the more.

[5.] The sins of others work for good as they make us more earnest in working out our salvation. When we see wicked men take such pains for hell, this makes us more diligent for heaven44. The wicked have nothing to encourage them, yet they sin. They risk shame and disgrace; they break through all opposition. Scripture is against them, and conscience is against them; there is a flaming sword in their way; yet they sin. Lam 5:9: “We get our bread at the risk of our lives.” Sinners eat the bread of wickedness at the risk of their souls. When godly hearts see the wicked so mad for the forbidden fruit, wearing themselves out in the devil’s service, they are the more emboldened and enlivened in the ways of God; they will take heaven, as it were, by storm. The wicked are swift dromedaries in sin (Jer 2:23); and do we creep like snails in religion? Will impure sinners do the devil more service than we do Christ? Will they make more haste to a prison than we do to a kingdom? Are they never weary of sinning, and are we weary of praying? Do we not have a better master than they? Are not the paths of virtue pleasant? Is there not joy in the way of duty, and heaven at the end? The activity of the sons of Belial in sin is a spur to the godly to make them mend their pace and run the faster to heaven.

[6.] The sins of others work for good as they are mirrors in which we may see our own hearts. Do we see a wicked, ungodly sinner? Behold a picture of our own hearts: so we would be if God left us. What is in other men’s practice is in our nature. Sin in the wicked is like fire on a beacon that flames and blazes out; sin in the godly is like fire in the embers. Christian, though you do not break out into a flame of scandal, yet you have no cause to boast, for there is much sin raked up in the embers of your nature. You have the root of bitterness in you, and you would bear as hellish fruit as anyone, if God did not either curb you by his power or change you by his grace.

[7.] The sins of others work for good as they are a means to make the people of God more thankful. When you+ see another infected with the plague, how thankful you+ are that God has preserved you+ from it! It is a good use that may be made even of the sins of others, to be more thankful. Why might God not have left us to the same “flood of reckless indiscretion”? Think to yourself, O Christian: why should God be more gracious to you than to another? Why should he take you out of the wild olive of nature, and not him? How this may make you adore free grace! What the Pharisee said boastingly, we may say thankfully. Luke 18:11: “God, I thank You that I am not like the other men—swindlers, evildoers, adulterers,” and so on. So we are to adore the riches of grace that we are not like others, drunkards, swearers, Sabbath-breakers. Every time we see men running riot in sin, we are to bless God that we are not such. If we see a madman, we bless God that it is not so with us. Much more, when we see others under the power of Satan, we are to give our thankful acknowledgment that it is not our condition.

[8.] The sins of others work for good as they are a means to make God’s people better. Christian, God can make you a gainer by another’s sin: the more unholy others are, the more holy you are. The roses that grow near garlic are the sweetest; so another’s foulness makes a Christian’s graces send out a more fragrant perfume. The more a wicked man gives himself to sin, the more a godly man gives himself to prayer. Ps 109:4: “but I give myself to prayer.”

[9.] The sins of others work for good as they give us occasion to do good. If there were no sinners, we could not be in such a position for service. The godly are often a means to convert the wicked: their prudent advice and godly example is a lure and bait to draw sinners to embrace the gospel. The disease of the patient works for the good of the physician: by emptying the patient of harmful, diseased matter, the physician enriches himself. So by turning sinners from the error of their way, our crown comes to be enlarged. Dan 12:3: “those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever.” Not like lamps or tapers, but sicut stellae, like the stars, forever. So we see the sins of others work for our good.

(2.) Our own sins will work for good. This must be understood with care. When I say that the sins of the godly work for good, I do not mean that there is the least good in sin. Sin is like poison, which corrupts the blood, infects the heart, and without a sovereign antidote brings death. Such is the venomous nature of sin: it is deadly and damning45. Sin is worse than hell. Yet God, by his mighty overruling power, makes sin in the outcome turn to the good of his people. God can make an antidote out of this poison. That is why St. Augustine has that golden saying, “God would never permit evil if he could not bring good out of evil.” The relics and remains of corruption in the saints work for good in several ways.

[1.] Sin makes them weary of this life. That sin is in the godly is sad, but that it is a burden to them is good. St. Paul’s afflictions (pardon the expression) were only a game to him compared with his sin. He rejoiced in tribulation (2 Cor 7:4). But how this bird of paradise wept and bemoaned himself under his sins! Rom 7:24: “Who will rescue me from this body of death?” A believer carries his sins as a prisoner carries his shackles. Oh how he longs for a jail delivery! This feeling of sin is good.

[2.] This indwelling of corruption makes the saints prize Christ more. He who feels his sin as a sick man feels his sickness, how welcome Christ the physician is to him! He who feels himself stung with sin, how precious the bronze serpent is to him! When Paul had cried out about a body of death, how thankful he was for Christ! Rom 7:25: “Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!” Christ’s blood saves from sin; it is the sacred ointment that kills this quicksilver.

[3.] Sin works for good as it is an occasion of setting the soul on six excellent duties.

1st. It sets the soul on searching itself. A child of God, being conscious of sin in himself, takes the candle and lantern of the word and searches into his heart. He wants to know the worst of himself, as a man who is sick in body wants to know the worst of his disease. Though our joy lies in the knowledge of our graces, yet there is some benefit in the knowledge of our corruptions. That is why Job prays, “Make me know my transgression” (Job 13:23). It is good to know our sins, so that we may not flatter ourselves or take our condition to be better than it is. It is good to find out our sins, so that they do not find us out.

2nd. The sin that remains in him sets a child of God on abasing himself. Sin is left in a godly man like a cancer in the breast or a hump on the back, to keep him from being proud. Gravel and dung are good to ballast a ship and keep it from overturning; the dung of sin helps to ballast the soul, so that it is not overturned with vainglory. We read of the spots of God’s children (Deut 32:5). When a godly man looks at his face in the mirror of Scripture and sees the spots of unbelief and hypocrisy, this makes the plumes of pride fall; they are humbling spots. It is a good use that may be made even of our sins, when they cause low thoughts of ourselves. Better is the sin that humbles me46 than the duty that makes me proud. Holy Bradford said these words of himself: “I am,” he says, “a painted hypocrite.” And Hooper said, “Lord, I am hell, and you are heaven.” From the thorn of sin the saints have gathered the grape of humility.

3rd. Sin sets a child of God on judging himself. He is sui judex; he passes sentence on himself. Prov 30:2: “I am more brutish than any man.” It is dangerous to judge others, but it is good to judge ourselves. 1 Cor 11:31: “if we judged ourselves properly, we would not come under judgment.” When a man has judged himself, Satan is put out of office. When Satan lays anything to a saint’s charge, the saint is able to answer back and say, “It is true, Satan, I am guilty of these sins, but I have already judged myself for them. And since I have condemned myself in the lower court of conscience, God will acquit me in the upper court of heaven.”

4th. Sin sets a child of God on conflict with himself. The spiritual self is in conflict with the carnal self. Gal 5:17: “the Spirit craves what is contrary to the flesh.” Our life is a wayfaring life and a warfaring life; there is a duel fought every day between the two seeds. A believer will not let sin have peaceable possession. If he cannot keep sin out, he will keep sin under. Though he cannot quite overcome, yet he is overcoming (Rev 2:7): τῶ νικῶντι, to him who is overcoming.

5th. Sin sets a child of God on watching himself. He knows sin is a traitor in his bosom, so he watches himself closely. A subtle heart needs a watchful eye. The heart is like a castle that is in danger of being assaulted every hour. This makes a child of God always stand sentry and keep a guard about his heart. A believer keeps a strict eye on himself, so that he may not fall into any scandalous enormity and so open a sluice to let all his comfort run out.

6th. Sin sets the soul on reforming itself47. A child of God does not only find out sin, but drives out sin. One foot he sets on the neck of his sins, and the other foot he turns to God’s testimonies (Ps 119:59). So the sins of the godly work for good: God makes the saints’ maladies their medicines.

But let no one abuse this doctrine. I do not say that sin works for good to an impenitent person; no, it works for his damnation. It is to those who love God. And as for you+ who are godly, I know you+ will not draw a wrong conclusion from this, either to make light of sin or to make bold with sin48. If you+ did so, God would make it cost you+ dearly. Remember David. He ventured presumptuously on sin, and what did he get? He lost his peace; he felt the terrors of the Almighty in his soul. Though he had every help to cheerfulness (he was a king, he was of a ruddy, sanguine complexion, he had skill in music), yet nothing could bring him comfort. He complains of his broken bones49 (Ps 51:8). And though he did at last come out of that dark cloud, yet some divines are of the opinion that he never recovered his full joy to his dying day. If any of God’s people should tamper with sin because God can turn it to good, though the Lord does not damn them, he may send them to hell in this life. He may put them into such bitter agonies and convulsions of soul as may fill them with horror and bring them near to despair. Let this be a flaming sword to keep them from coming near the forbidden tree.

And so I have shown that both the best things and the worst things, by the overruling hand of the great God, work together for the good of the saints.

23. καὶ πάντα περιτρέπει ὁ θεὸς εἰς ἀγαθά. [And God turns all things to good.] Aecumon.

24. Evil things in their own nature do not work together, but work against.

25. Non dixit Job, Deus dedit, Diabolus abstulit.

33. ὁ διάβολος ἐπιθηρᾶται πλέον, ὅταν ἴδῃ τὰ φορτία τῆς ἀρετῆς συγκείμενα, καὶ πολὺν τὸν ὄγκον. [The devil hunts the harder when he sees the loads of virtue piled together, and their great bulk.] Chrysost.

[As fires are put out by fires, poisons are driven out by poisons, and the heats of fevers are broken by medicinal heats, so nothing hinders sins from being cured by sins.] Augustine contra Pelag.
