Chapter V

Showing the Reason for the Proposition.

The great reason why all things will work for good50 is the near and dear relation that God has to his people. The Lord has made a covenant with them: “They will be My people, and I will be their God” (Jer 32:38). By virtue of this compact all things do, and must, work for good to them. “I am God, your God” (Ps 50:7). This word אלהיךָ, your God, is the sweetest word in the Bible. It implies the best relations, and it is impossible that there should be these relations between God and his people and everything not work for their good. This expression, I am your God, implies:

1. The relation of a physician: I am your physician. God is 1. a skillful physician, so he knows what is best51. God observes the different temperaments of men and knows what will work most effectually. Some are of a sweeter disposition and are drawn by mercy; others are more rugged and knotty pieces, and these God deals with in a more forceful way. Some things are preserved in sugar, some in brine. God does not deal alike with all; he has trials for the strong and cordials for the weak. 2. God is a faithful physician, so he will turn all to the best. If he does not give to you ad voluntatem, it will be ad sanitatem52; if God does not give you what you like, he will give you what you need. A physician does not take such care to please the patient’s taste as to cure his disease. We complain that such sore trials lie on us. Let us remember that God is our physician, so he works to heal us rather than to humor us. God’s dealings with his children, though they are sharp, are safe, and they aim at a cure: “so that in the end He might do you good” (Deut 8:16).

This word, your God, implies the relation of a father. A father loves his child, so whether it is a smile or a stroke, it is for the good of the child. I am your God, your Father, so all I do is for your good: “Just as a man chastens his son, so the LORD your God chastens you” (Deut 8:5). God’s chastening is not to destroy but to reform. God cannot hurt his children, for 1. he is a tender-hearted Father: “As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him” (Ps 103:13). Will a father seek the ruin of his child, the child who came from his own body and bears his image? All his care and planning is for his child. On whom does he settle the inheritance but on his child? God is tender-hearted, the “Father of mercies” (2 Cor 1:3). He begets all the mercies and tender affections in created things. 2. He is an everlasting Father (Isa 9:6). He was our Father from eternity: before we were children, God was our Father, and he will be our Father to eternity. A father provides for his child while he lives; but the father dies, and then the child may be exposed to injury. But God never ceases to be a Father. You who are a believer have a Father who never dies, and if God is your Father, you can never be undone: all things must necessarily work for your good.

3. This word, your God, carries the relation of a husband, and this is a near and sweet relation. The husband seeks the good of his spouse; he would be a man without natural affection who set out to destroy his wife: “No one ever hated his own body” (Eph 5:29). There is a marriage relation between God and his people53: “Your husband is your Maker” (Isa 54:5). God loves his people with his whole heart (Isa 43:4). He engraves them on the palms of his hands (Isa 49:16). He sets them as a seal on his breast (Song 8:6). He will give kingdoms for their ransom (Isa 43:3). This shows how near they lie to his heart. If he is a husband whose heart is captured with love, then he will seek the good of his spouse: either he will ward off an injury, or he will turn it to the best.

4. This word, your God, implies the relation of a friend: “This is my friend” (Song 5:16). A friend is animae dimidium (as Augustine says), half of one’s self. He is eager and inquiring how he may do his friend good; he promotes his friend’s welfare as his own. Jonathan risked the king’s displeasure for his friend David (1 Sam 19:4). God is our friend, so he will turn all things to our good. There are false friends; Christ was betrayed by a friend. But God is the best friend.

(1.) He is a faithful friend: “Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God” (Deut 7:9). 1. He is faithful in his love. He gave his very heart to us when he gave the Son out of his bosom; here was a pattern of love without a parallel. 2. He is faithful in his promises: “God, who cannot lie, promised” (Titus 1:2). He may change his promise, but he cannot break it. 3. He is faithful in his dealings. When he is afflicting, he is faithful: “In faithfulness You have afflicted me” (Ps 119:75). He is sifting us and refining us like silver (Ps 66:10).

(2.) He is an unchangeable friend: “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you” (Heb 13:5). There are five seals set to that promise, οὐ, μὴ, οὐδ’, οὐ, μὴ [five words for “not”]. Friends often fail in a pinch. Many deal with their friends as women do with their flowers: while they are fresh they put them in their bosoms, but when they begin to wither they throw them away. Or they deal with them as the traveler does with the sundial. If the sun shines on the dial, the traveler will step out of the road and look at the dial; but if the sun does not shine on it, he will ride by and never take any notice of it. So if prosperity shines on men, their friends will look at them; but if there is a cloud of adversity on them, they will not come near them. But God is a friend forever: Never will I leave you. Though David walked through the shadow of death, he knew he had a friend beside him: “I will fear no evil, for You are with me” (Ps 23:4). God never wholly takes his love away from his people. It is amicitia immortalis54 [an immortal friendship]: “He loved them ἐις τέλος, to the very end” (John 13:1). God being such a friend, he will make all things work for our good. There is no friend who will not seek the good of his friend.

5. This word, your God, carries a still nearer relation, the relation between the head and the members. There is a mystical union between Christ and the saints. He is called κεφαλὴ, the head of the church (Eph 5:23). Does not the head take care for the good of the body? The head guides the body and feels with it; it is the fountain of the spirits; it sends out influence and comfort into the body. All the parts of the head are placed for the good of the body. The eye is set, as it were, in the watchtower; it stands sentinel to spy any danger that may come to the body, and to prevent it. The tongue is both a taster and an orator. If the body is a microcosm, or little world, the head is the sun in this world, from which comes the light of reason. The head is placed for the good of the body. Christ and the saints make one mystical body. Our head is in heaven, and surely he will not allow his body to be hurt, but will take care for its safety, and make all things work for the good of the mystical body.

50. Reason.

51. οὐκ οὕτως ἴσμεν τὸ συμφέρον ἡμῖν ὡς αὐτὸς ἐπίσταται. [We do not know what is good for us as well as he knows it.] Chrysost.

52. Augustine.

53. Anima fidelis Deum habet sponsum. [The faithful soul has God for its bridegroom.] Gulielm. Paris.

54. Augustine.

Chapter VI

The Inferences Drawn from the Proposition. A Use of Information.

1. If all things work for good, learn from this55 that there is a providence. Things do not work by themselves; God sets them working for good.56 God is the great disposer of all events and outcomes; he sets everything working. “His kingdom rules over all” (Ps 103:19); this is meant of his providential kingdom. Things in the world are not governed by second causes, by the counsels of men, or by the stars and planets, but by divine providence. Providence is Regina mundi, the queen and governess of the world. There are three things in providence: 1. πρόγνωσις, God’s foreknowing; 2. προορισμὸς, God’s determining; 3. διοίκησις, God’s directing all things to their ends and outcomes. Whatever things work in the world, God sets them working. We read in the first chapter of Ezekiel of wheels, and eyes in the wheels, and the moving of the wheels. The wheels are the whole universe; the eyes in the wheels are God’s providence; the moving of the wheels is the hand of providence turning all things here below. What some call a chance killing is nothing else but the result of providence57

Learn to adore providence. Providence has an influence on all things here below. It is providence that mixes the ingredients and makes up the whole compound.

2. It shows us the happy condition of every child of God: All things work for his good, the best and the worst things: “Light dawns in the darkness for the upright” (Ps 112:4)58. The darkest, cloudiest providences of God have some sunshine in them59. What a blessed condition a true believer is in! When he dies he goes to God, and while he lives everything will do him good. Affliction is for his good. What hurt does the fire do to the gold? It only purifies it. What hurt does the fan do to the grain? It only separates the chaff from it. What hurt do leeches do to the body? They only suck out the bad blood. God never uses his staff except to beat out the dust. Affliction does what the word often will not do: it opens the ear to correction (Job 36:10). When God lays men on their backs, then they look up to heaven. God’s striking his people is like the musician striking the viol, which makes it give out a melodious sound. How much good comes to the saints by affliction! When they are pounded and broken, they give out their sweetest smell. Affliction is a bitter root, but it bears sweet fruit: “it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness” (Heb 12:11). Affliction is the highway to heaven; though it is flinty and thorny, yet it is the nearest way. Poverty will starve our sins; sickness will make grace more healthy60 (2 Cor 4:16). Reproach will cause “the Spirit of glory and of God” to rest on us (1 Pet 4:14): ἐγκλήματα, ἐγκωμία [reproaches are praises]. Death will stop the bottle of tears and open the gate of paradise. A believer’s dying day is his ascension day to glory. That is why the saints have put their afflictions in the inventory of their riches (Heb 11:26). Themistocles, banished from his own country, afterward grew in favor with the king of Egypt, and on this he said, Periissem, nisi periissem, “I would have perished, if I had not perished.” So a child of God may say, If I had not been afflicted, I would have been destroyed; if my health and estate had not been lost, my soul would have been lost.

3.61 See, then, what an encouragement there is here to become godly! All things will work for good. Oh that this might tempt the world to fall in love with religion! Can there be a greater lodestone to piety? Can anything prevail with us more to be good than this, All things will work for our good? Religion is the true philosopher’s stone, which turns everything into gold. Take the sourest part of religion, the suffering part, and there is comfort in it. God sweetens sufferings with joy; he candies our wormwood with sugar. Oh how this may bribe us to godliness! “Acquaint yourself with Him and be at peace; thereby good will come to you” (Job 22:21). No man ever came away a loser by his acquaintance with God. Thereby good will come to you: abundance of good, the sweet distillings of grace, the hidden manna, yes, everything will work for good. Oh then get acquainted with God; take up his cause as your own.62

4. It shows us the miserable condition of wicked men. To those who are godly, evil things work for good; to those who are evil, good things work for hurt: illis qui oderunt deum, etiam bona cedunt in malum [to those who hate God, even good things turn to evil].

(1.) Temporal good things work for hurt to the wicked: riches and prosperity63. They are not munera [gifts] but insidiae [snares], as Seneca says. Worldly things are given to the wicked as Michal was given to David, for a snare (1 Sam 18:21). The vulture draws sickness from a perfume, and so do the wicked from the sweet perfume of prosperity. Their mercies are like poisoned bread given to dogs. Their tables are lavishly spread, but there is a hook under the bait: “May their table become a snare” (Ps 69:22). All their enjoyments are like Israel’s quails, which were sauced with the wrath of God (Num 11:33).—Foenus pecuniae, funus animae [The interest of money is the funeral of the soul].— Pride and luxury are the twins of prosperity: “You grew fat … then he forsook God” (Deut 32:15)64. Riches are not only the spider’s web, unprofitable, but the cockatrice’s egg, deadly: “wealth hoarded to the hurt of its owner” (Eccl 5:13). Et transeunt, et vulnerant [They both pass away and wound]65. The common mercies wicked men have are not lodestones to draw them nearer to God, but millstones to sink them deeper in hell (1 Tim 6:9). Their delicious dainties are like Haman’s banquet. After all their lordly fare, death will bring in the bill, and they must pay it in hell.

(2.) Spiritual good things work for hurt to the wicked; from the flower of heavenly blessings they suck poison.

[1.] The ministers of God work for their hurt. The same wind that blows one ship to the harbor blows another ship onto a rock. The same breath in the ministry that blows a godly man to heaven blows a profane sinner to hell. Those who come with the word of life in their mouth are yet to many an odor of death: “Make the hearts of this people calloused; deafen their ears” (Isa 6:10). The prophet was sent on a sad errand, to preach their funeral sermon. Wicked men are worse for preaching: they “hate the one who reproves in the gate” (Amos 5:10). Sinners grow more set in sin. Let God say what he will, they will do what they please: “As for the word you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you!” (Jer 44:16). The word preached is not healing to them, but hardening. And how dreadful this is, for men to be sunk into hell with sermons!

[2.] Prayer works for their hurt: “The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable to the LORD” (Prov 15:8). A wicked man is in a great strait: if he does not pray, he sins; if he prays, he sins: “May his prayer become sin” (Ps 109:7). It would be a sad judgment if all the food a man ate turned to poison and bred diseases in the body. So it is with a wicked man: the prayer that should do him good works for his hurt. He prays against sin, and sins against his prayer. His duties are tainted with atheism and fly-blown with hypocrisy; God abhors them.

[3.] The Lord’s Supper works for their hurt: “You+ cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too. Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy?” (1 Cor 10:21, 22). Some of the Jews kept their idol feasts, yet would come to the Lord’s table. The apostle says, Are you+ provoking the Lord to wrath? Profane persons feast with their sins, yet will come to feast at the Lord’s table. This is to provoke God. To a sinner there is death in the cup; he “eats and drinks damnation on himself” (1 Cor 11:29). So the Lord’s Supper works for hurt to impenitent sinners. After the morsel, the devil enters.

[4.] Christ himself works for hurt to hardened sinners. He is λίθος προσκόμματος, “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (1 Pet 2:8). He is so not of his own nature but only as the occasion of it, through the depravity of men’s hearts: instead of believing in him, they take offense at him. The sun, though pure and pleasant in its own nature, is hurtful to sore eyes. Jesus Christ is set for the fall as well as the rising of many (Luke 2:34). Sinners stumble at a Savior and pluck death from the tree of life. As chemical oils restore some patients but destroy others, so the blood of Christ, though to some it is healing, is to others damning. Here is the unparalleled misery of those who live and die in sin: the best things work for their hurt; cordials themselves kill.

5. See here the wisdom of God,66 who can make the worst things imaginable turn to the good of the saints. By a divine chemistry he can extract gold out of dross. ὦ βάθος: “O, the depth of … the wisdom … of God!” (Rom 11:33). It is God’s great design to display the wonder of his wisdom. The Lord made Joseph’s prison a step to promotion. There was no way for Jonah to be saved but by being swallowed up. God allowed the Egyptians to hate Israel (Ps 105:25), and this was the means of their deliverance. St. Paul was bound with a chain, and the chain that bound him was a means to spread the gospel (Phil 1:12). This wise physician can make an antidote out of the viper. God enriches by impoverishing; he increases grace by diminishing an estate. When created things go further from us, it is so that Christ may come nearer to us. God works in strange ways. He brings order out of confusion and harmony out of discord. He often makes use of unjust men to do what is just. He is wise in heart (Job 9:4). He can reap his glory out of men’s fury67 (Ps 76:10). Either the wicked will not do the hurt they intend, or they will do the good they do not intend. God often helps when there is least hope, and saves his people in the way by which they think he will destroy them. He made use of the high priests’ malice and Judas’s treason to redeem the world. God sometimes has much ado to please us. Through rash passion we are apt to find fault with things that happen, which is as if an unlearned man should criticize philosophy, or a blind man find fault with the work in a landscape: “Empty man would be wise” (Job 11:12). Silly creatures will be finding fault with providence and calling the wisdom of God to the bar of reason. God’s ways are untraceable (Rom 11:33). They are to be wondered at rather than fathomed. There is no providence of God that does not have either a mercy or a wonder in it. How astonishing and infinite is that wisdom that makes the most adverse and perplexing dealings work for the good of his children!

6. How little cause we have, then, to be discontented at outward trials and emergencies!68 What? Discontented at what will do us good? All things will work for good. There are no sins God’s people are more subject to than unbelief and impatience. They are ready either to faint through unbelief or to fret through impatience. When men break out against God in discontent and impatience, it is a sign that they do not believe this text. Discontent is an ungrateful sin, because we have more mercies than afflictions; and it is an irrational sin, because afflictions work for good. Discontent is a sin that pushes us into sin: “Do not fret yourself; it leads only to doing evil” (Ps 37:8). He who frets will be ready to do evil. Fretting Jonah was sinning Jonah (Jonah 4:9). The devil blows the coals of passion and discontent, and then warms himself at the fire. Oh let us not nourish this angry viper in our breast. Let this text breed patience: “All things work together for good to those who love God.” Shall we be discontented at what works for our good69? If a friend threw a bag of money at another man, and in throwing it broke his head, the man would not be much troubled, seeing that by this means he has got a bag of money. So the Lord may bruise us by afflictions, but it is to enrich us. These afflictions are working for us a weight of glory; and shall we be discontented?

7. See here that scripture fulfilled: “Surely God is good to Israel” (Ps 73:1).70 When a man looks on adverse providences, and sees the Lord covering his people with ashes and making them drunk with wormwood (Lam 3:15), he would be ready to call the love of God into question, and to say that he has dealt harshly with his people. Oh no, yet God is good to Israel, because he makes all things work for good. Is he not a good God who turns all to good? He works out sin and works in grace; is this not good? “When we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined so that we will not be condemned with the world” (1 Cor 11:32). The hell of affliction is to save us from the hell of damnation. Let us always justify God. However bad our outward condition is, let us say, Yet God is good.

8. See what cause the saints have to be frequent in the work of thanksgiving!71 Christians are lacking in this: though they are much in petition, they are little in thanksgiving. The apostle says, ἐν παντὶ, “Give thanks in everything” (1 Thess 5:18). Why so? Because God makes everything work for our good. We will thank the physician though he gives us a bitter pill that makes us sick, because it is to make us well. We will thank any man who does us a good turn; and shall we not be thankful to God, who makes everything work for good to us? God loves a thankful Christian. Job thanked God when he took everything away: “The LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21). Many will thank God when he gives; Job thanks him when he takes away, because he knew God would work good out of it. We read of saints with harps in their hands (Rev 14:2), an emblem of praise. We will meet many Christians who have tears in their eyes and complaints in their mouths, but few with harps in their hands, who praise God in affliction. To be thankful in affliction is a work peculiar to a saint. Every bird can sing in spring, but some birds will sing in the dead of winter. Almost everyone can be thankful in prosperity, but a true saint can be thankful in adversity. A good Christian will bless God not only at sunrise but at sunset. Well may we have a psalm of thankfulness in the worst that befalls us, because all things work for good72. Oh be much in blessing God. We will thank one who befriends us. —

9. If the worst things work for good to a believer, what will the best things do, Christ and heaven? How much more will these work for good? If the cross has so much good in it,73 what does the crown have? If such precious clusters grow in Golgotha, how delicious is the fruit that grows in Canaan? If there is any sweetness in the waters of Marah, what is there in the wine of paradise? If God’s rod has honey at the end of it, what does his golden scepter have? If the bread of affliction tastes so good, what is manna? What is the heavenly ambrosia? If God’s blow and stroke work for good, what will the smiles of his face do? If grapes may be gathered from thorns, what fruit will the tree of life yield? If temptations and sufferings have matter for joy in them, what will glory have? If there is so much good out of evil, what then is that good where there will be no evil? If God’s chastening mercies are so great, what will his crowning mercies be? “Therefore comfort one another with these words.”

10. If God makes all things turn to our good,74 how right it is that we should make all things serve his glory! “Do it all to the glory of God” (1 Cor 10:31). The angels glorify God; they sing divine anthems of praise. How then ought man to glorify him, for whom God has done more than for the angels! He has honored us above them by uniting our nature with the Godhead. Christ has died for us, and not for the angels. The Lord has given to us not only out of the common stock of his bounty, but he has enriched us with covenant blessings; he has bestowed on us his Spirit. He plans for our welfare; he makes everything work for our good. Free grace has laid a plan for our salvation. If God seeks our good, shall we not seek his glory?

Question. How can we properly be said to glorify God? He is infinite in his perfections and can receive no increase from us.

Answer. It is true that in a strict sense we cannot bring glory to God, but in an evangelical sense we may. When we do all that lies in us to lift up God’s name in the world, and cause others to have high and reverent thoughts of God, the Lord counts this as glorifying him; just as a man is said to dishonor God when he causes the name of God to be spoken evil of.

Question. In how many ways are we said to advance God’s glory? Answer. In three ways. 1. When we aim at his glory75; when we make him the first in our thoughts and the last in our end. As all the rivers run into the sea, and all the lines meet in the center, so all our actions end and center in God. 2. We advance God’s glory by being fruitful in grace: “This is to My Father’s glory, that you+ bear much fruit” (John 15:8). Barrenness brings dishonor on God. We glorify God when we grow in beauty like the lily, in tallness like the cedar, in fruitfulness like the vine. The spouse’s breasts were like “clusters of grapes” (Song 7:7).— 3. We glorify God when we give the praise and glory of all we do to God. It was an excellent and humble saying of the king of Sweden: he feared that the people’s giving him the glory that was due to God would remove him before the work was done. When the silkworm weaves her intricate work, she hides herself under the silk and is not seen. When we have done our best, we must vanish in our own thoughts and transfer the glory of all to God: “I worked harder than all of them” (1 Cor 15:10). One would think this saying smacked of pride. But the apostle pulls the crown off his own head and sets it on the head of free grace: “yet not I, but the grace of God that was with me.” Constantine used to write the name of Christ over his door, and so should we over our duties.

So let us endeavor to make the name of God glorious and renowned. If God seeks our good, let us seek his glory. If he makes all things serve our edification, let us make all things serve his exaltation. So much for the first part of the text, the privilege.

75. ὁ πάντα ποιῶν διὰ τὸν θεὸν πάντως ἀπολαύσεται τῆς ἀμοιβῆς· [He who does all things for God’s sake will surely enjoy the reward.]

The Breathings of Love

Chapter VII

Showing the nature, cause, kinds, properties, and degree of love to God.

2. I proceed to the second general branch of the text: the persons who have a share in this privilege. They are qualified in two ways.

1. They are lovers of God: “all things work together for good τοῖς ἀγαπῶσι τὸν θεὸν, to those who love God.” Those who despise and hate God have no lot or part in this privilege. It is “the children’s bread”; it belongs only to those who love God. Because love is the very heart and spirit of religion, I will enlarge on it all the more. To discuss it further, I will make these five things clear.

  1. The nature of love to God.
  2. The ground of love to God.
  3. The kinds of love to God.
  4. The properties of love to God.
  5. The degree of love to God.

The Nature of Love

1. The nature of divine love. Love is an expansion of the soul, or the kindling of the affections, by which a Christian breathes after God as the supreme and sovereign good. Augustine, in his second volume, calls love pondus animae [the weight of the soul]. Love is to the soul what the weights are to a clock: it sets the soul going toward God. It is the wing by which we fly to heaven. By love we cling to God, as the needle clings to the magnet.

The Ground of Love

2. The ground of love to God is knowledge. Ignoti nulla cupido: we cannot love what we do not know. For our love to be drawn out to God, we must know these three things in him.

(1.) A fullness (Col 1:19). He has a fullness of grace to cleanse us and of glory to crown us. It is a fullness not only of sufficiency but of overflowing. He is a sea of goodness without bottom and banks.

(2.) A freeness. Fluit acrius amne perenni [it flows more freely than an ever-running river]. God has an inborn readiness to give out mercy and grace. He drops like the honeycomb (Rev 22:17): “Let the one who desires the water of life drink freely.” God does not require us to bring money with us, only appetite.

(3.) Ownership. We must know that this fullness in God is ours (Ps 48:14): “This God is our God.” Here is the ground of love: Deity and ownership.

The Kinds of Love

3. The kinds of love. I will divide them into these three.

(1.) There is a love of appreciation, when we set a high value on God as the most sublime and infinite good. We so esteem God that if we have him, we do not care though we lack everything else. The stars vanish when the sun appears. So all created things vanish in our thoughts when the Sun of righteousness shines in his full splendor (Song 1:13): “My beloved is to me a sachet of myrrh,” and “a cluster of henna blossoms.”

(2.) A love of good pleasure and delight. So Aquinas defines love as complacentia amantis in amato [the delight of the lover in the beloved], as a man takes delight in a friend whom he loves. The soul that loves God rejoices in him as its treasure and rests in him as its center. The heart is so set on God that it desires nothing more (John 14:8): “Show us the Father, and that will be enough for us.”

(3.) A love of benevolence, which is wishing well to the cause of God76. He who is bound in affection to his friend wishes him every happiness. This is loving God: when we are his well-wishers and desire that his cause may prevail. Our wish and prayer is that his name may be held in honor, and that his gospel, which is “the rod of his strength,” may, like Aaron’s rod, blossom and bring forth almonds.

The Properties of Love

4. The properties of love.

(1.) Our love to God must be entire, and that ex parte subjecti, with regard to the subject: it must be with the whole heart (Mark 12:30): “Love the Lord your God ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας, with all your heart.” Under the old law, a high priest was not to marry a widow or a harlot: not a widow, because he did not have her first love, and not a harlot, because he did not have all her love. God will have the whole heart. Hos 10:2: “Their heart is divided.” The true mother would not have the child divided, and God will not have the heart divided. God will not be a lodger, with only one room in the heart while all the other rooms are let out to sin. It must be an entire love.

(2.) It must be a sincere love (Eph 6:24): “Grace to all who love our Lord Jesus ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ, in sincerity.” Sincere, quasi sine cera [as if without wax]: it alludes to honey that is pure and has no wax in it. Our love to God is sincere when it is pure and free of self-interest. The schoolmen call this amor amicitiae, a love of friendship. We must love Christ propter Christum (as Augustine says), for himself, as we love sweet wine for its taste. God’s beauty and love must be the two magnets that draw our love to him. Alexander had two friends, Hephaestion and Craterus. “Hephaestion,” he said, “loves me because I am Alexander; Craterus loves me because I am King Alexander.” The one loved his person, the other his benefits. Many love God because he gives them grain and wine, and not for his own excellencies. Lycurgus wanted young women to be married without a dowry, so that their husbands would marry them purely for love. We must love God more for what he is than for what he gives. True love is not mercenary. You do not need to hire a mother to love her child. A soul deeply in love with God does not need to be hired with rewards; he cannot help loving him for the radiant beauty that sparkles forth in him.

(3.) It must be a fervent love. The Hebrew word for love, אהבא, signifies ardent affection. Saints must be seraphim, burning in holy love. To love someone coldly is the same as not to love him. The sun shines as hot as it can. Our love to God must be intense and vehement, like the “burning coals of the broom tree,” which are the hottest and fiercest (Ps 120:4). Our love to passing things must be cool; we must love quasi non, “as if we did not” (1 Cor 7:30)77. But our love to God must flame forth. The bride was amore perculsa, “faint with love” for Christ (Song 2:5). We can never love God as he deserves. As God’s punishing us is less than we deserve (Ezra 9:13), so our loving him is less than he deserves.

(4.) Love to God must be active. It is like fire, the most active element. It is called “your labor of love” (1 Thess 1:3). Love is no idle grace. It sets the head planning for God and the feet running in the ways of his commandments: “Christ’s love compels” (2 Cor 5:14). Claims of love are not enough. True love is seen not only at the tongue’s end but at the fingers’ end; it is “the labor of love.” Those living creatures in Ezek 1:8 had wings, and hands under their wings. That is an emblem of a good Christian: he has not only the wings of faith to fly with, but hands under his wings. He works by love; he spends and is spent for Christ.

(5.) Love is generous. It has love-tokens to give (1 Cor 13:4): “Love χρηστεύεται, is kind.” Love has not only a smooth tongue but a kind heart. David’s heart was on fire with love to God, and he would not offer to God what cost him nothing (2 Sam 24:24). Love is full not only of benevolence but of beneficence. Love that enlarges the heart never tightens the hand. He who loves Christ will be generous to his members. He will be “eyes to the blind” and “feet to the lame.” The backs and bellies of the poor will be the furrows where he sows the golden seeds of generosity. Some say they love God, but their love is lame in one hand: they give nothing to good uses. Faith does indeed deal with things invisible, but God hates love that is invisible. Love is like new wine, which must have a vent; it vents itself in good works. The apostle speaks to the honor of the Corinthians that they gave to the poor saints not only according to their ability but beyond it (2 Cor 8:3). Love is bred at court; it is a noble, bountiful grace.

(6.) Love to God is special, set apart for him alone. He who loves God gives him a love that he gives to no one else. God gives his children a love he does not give to the wicked, an electing, adopting love. In the same way a gracious heart gives God a special, distinguishing love that no one else shares in (2 Cor 11:2): “I betrothed you+ to one husband, to present you+ as a pure virgin to Christ.” A wife betrothed to a husband gives him a love she has for no one else; she does not part with her married love to anyone but her husband. So a saint betrothed to Christ gives him a love peculiar to him, a love that cannot be shared with any other: a love joined with adoration. Not only the love is given to God, but the soul (Song 4:12): “My sister, my bride, you are a garden locked up.” The heart of a believer is Christ’s garden. The flower growing in it is love mixed with divine worship, and this flower is for Christ alone to smell. The bride keeps the key of the garden, so that no one may come there but Christ.

(7.) Love to God is permanent. It is like the fire the Vestal Virgins kept in Rome: it does not go out. True love boils over, but it does not give over. As love to God is sincere without hypocrisy, so it is constant without apostasy. Love is like the pulse of the body, always beating. It is not a flash flood but a spring. Wicked men are constant in their love to their sins: neither shame, nor sickness, nor fear of hell will make them give up their sins. So nothing can hinder a Christian’s love to God. Nothing can conquer love, no difficulties or opposition (Song 8:6): “Love is as strong as the grave.” The grave swallows up the strongest bodies, and love swallows up the strongest difficulties (Song 8:7): “Mighty waters cannot quench love,” neither the sweet waters of pleasure nor the bitter waters of persecution. Love to God holds firm to death (Eph 3:17): “being rooted and grounded in love.” Light things, like chaff and feathers, are quickly blown away, but a tree that is rooted stands through the storm. He who is rooted in love endures. True love never ends except with life.

The Degrees of Love

5. The degrees of love. We must love God above all other objects78 (Ps 73:25): “On earth I desire nothing besides You.” God is the essence of all good things; he is good in the highest degree. Now the soul sees a surpassing excellence in God, and wonders at that constellation of all excellencies in him, and so it is carried out in love to him in the highest degree. “The measure of our love to God,” says Bernard, “is to love him without measure”79. God, who is the chief of our happiness, must have the chief of our affections (Song 8:2): “I would give you spiced wine to drink, the juice of my pomegranates.” If the bride has any love better than the rest, a cup more juicy and spiced, Christ shall drink of that. Created things may have the milk of our love, but God must have the cream. Love to God must be above all other things, as oil floats above water.

(1.) We must love God more than relatives. Take the case of Abraham’s offering up Isaac. Isaac was the son of his old age; no doubt he loved him wholly and doted on him. But God said, “Abraham, offer up your son.” It was a thing that might seem to baffle not only his reason but his faith, for the Messiah was to come from Isaac; if Isaac were cut off, where would the world have a Mediator? Yet such was the strength of Abraham’s faith, and the ardor of his love to God, that he would take the sacrificing knife and let out Isaac’s blood. Our blessed Savior tells us of hating father and mother (Luke 14:26). Christ would not have us without natural affection. But if our dearest relatives lie in our way and would hinder us from Christ, we must either step over them or tread on them (Deut 33:9). Though some few drops of love may run aside to our kindred and in-laws, the full torrent must run out after Christ. Relatives may lie in the bosom, but Christ must lie in the heart.

(2.) We must love God more than possessions. Heb 10:34: “You+ joyfully accepted the confiscation of your+ property.” They were glad they had anything to lose for Christ. If the world is laid in one scale and Christ in the other, he must weigh heaviest. And is it so with us? Does God have the highest room in our affections? Plutarch says that when a dictator was appointed in Rome, all other authority was suspended for the time. So when the love of God bears sway in the heart, all other love is suspended, and is as nothing compared with this love.

76. Φιλεῖν ἐστι βούλεσθαι τινὶ ὁ ὄντα ἀγαθὰ, etc. [To love is to wish for someone what one thinks good.] Aristotle.

77. Non jubet Apostolus ut mundana haec abjiciamus, sed ne simus hisce fluxis rebus immersi; tunc enim non possidemus, sed ab illis possidemur. [The apostle does not command us to throw these worldly things away, but not to be sunk in these passing things; for then we do not possess them, but are possessed by them.] Beza.

78. Minus Domine te amat, qui aliquid tecum amat. [He loves you less, Lord, who loves anything along with you.] Augustine.

79. Modus diligendi Deum, est diligere Deum sine modo. Bernard.

Chapter VIII

Containing a sharp rebuke to those who do not love God.

Use 1. This may serve as a sharp rebuke to those who do not have a dram of love to God in their hearts.80 Are there such wretches alive? He who does not love God, aut lapis est, aut belluae [is either a stone or a beast]; he is a beast with a man’s head. O wretch, do you live on God every day, and yet not love him? Suppose a man had a friend who kept him supplied with money and gave him all his allowance. Would he not be worse than a barbarian if he did not respect and honor that friend? Such a friend is God. He gives you your breath; he gives you a livelihood. And will you not love him? You would love your prince if he saved your life, and will you not love God, who gives you your life? What magnet is as powerful to draw love as the blessed Deity? He is blind whom beauty does not attract; he is stupid who is not drawn by the cords of love. When the body is cold and has no heat in it, it is a sign of death. That man is dead who has no heat of love to God in his soul. How can he expect love from God, when he shows no love to him? Will God ever lay in his bosom such a viper, one that spits out the poison of malice and hostility against him?

This rebuke falls heavily on the atheists of this age. They are so far from loving God that they do all they can to spite him. “Like Sodom they flaunt their sin” (Isa 3:9). “They set their mouths against the heavens”81 in pride and blasphemy, and openly defy God. These are monsters in nature, devils in the shape of men. Let them read their doom in 1 Cor 16:22: “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha”82; that is, let him be accursed from God until Christ’s coming to judgment83. Let him be heir to a curse while he lives, and on the dreadful day of the Lord let him hear that heart-rending sentence pronounced against him: “Depart from Me, you who are cursed.”

80. Use 1. Reproof.

81. Ps 73:9.

82. Idem significat vox חרם apud Hebraeos. [The word חרם means the same among the Hebrews.]

83. τὸ ἀνάθεμα παντελῶς τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἀποκόπτει. [The anathema cuts a man off from Christ entirely.] Chrysostom, On Anathema.

Chapter IX

Laying open the signs, or fruits, of love to God.

Use 2. Let us test ourselves impartially84 to see whether we are among those who love God. To settle this (for our love will best be seen by its fruits), I will set down fourteen signs, or fruits, of love to God. It concerns us closely to search whether any of these fruits grow in our garden.

1. The first fruit of love is the mind’s musing on God. The thoughts of a man who is in love85 are always on the one he loves. He who loves God is enraptured and carried away with the contemplation of God (Ps 139:18): “When I awake, I am still with You.” Thoughts are like travelers in the mind. David’s thoughts kept to the road to heaven: “I am still with You.” God is the treasure, and where the treasure is, there the heart is. By this we may test our love to God. What are our thoughts most on? Can we say we are enraptured with delight when we think of God? Have our thoughts got wings? Have they flown on high? Do we contemplate Christ and glory? Oh, how far are they from being lovers of God who hardly ever think of God! Ps 10:4: “In all his thoughts there is no God.” A sinner crowds God out of his thoughts. He never thinks of God except with horror, as the prisoner thinks of the judge.

2. The second fruit of love is desire for communion.86 Love desires closeness and fellowship (Ps 84:2): “My heart and my flesh cry out for the living God.” King David was shut out from the house of God, where the tabernacle was (the visible token of his presence). Now he breathes after God, and in a holy passion of desire cries out for the living God. Lovers want to be talking together. If we love God, we prize his ordinances, because there we meet with God. He speaks to us in his word, and we speak to him in prayer. By this let us examine our love to God. Do we desire close communion with God? Lovers cannot be apart for long. Those who love God have a holy fondness; they do not know how to be away from him. They can do without anything but God’s presence. They can do without health and friends, they can do without a full table, but they cannot do without God. Ps 143:7: “Do not hide Your face from me, or I will be like those who descend to the Pit.” Lovers have their λειποθυμίαι, their fainting fits. David was ready to faint away and die when he had no sight of God. Those who love God cannot be content with having ordinances unless they may enjoy God in them. That would be to lick the glass and not the honey.

What shall we say to those who can live their whole lives without God? They think God is the thing they can best spare. They complain that they lack health and trade, but not that they lack God. Wicked men are not acquainted with God, and how can they love when they are not acquainted? Indeed, what is worse, they do not desire to be acquainted with God (Job 21:14): “They say to God: ‘Leave us alone! For we have no desire to know Your ways.’” Sinners shun acquaintance with God; they count his presence a burden. And are these lovers of God? Does that woman love her husband who cannot bear to be in his presence?

3. The third fruit of love is grief. Where there is love to God,87 there is grieving for our sins of unkindness against him. A child who loves his father cannot help weeping for offending him. The heart that burns with love melts in tears. “Oh, that I should abuse the love of so dear a Savior! Did not my Lord suffer enough on the cross? Must I make him suffer more? Shall I give him more gall and vinegar to drink? How disloyal and unworthy I have been! How I have grieved his Spirit, trampled on his royal commands, and slighted his blood!” This opens a vein of godly sorrow and makes the heart bleed afresh. Matt 26:75: “Peter … went outside and wept bitterly.” Peter thought how dearly Christ had loved him. He had been taken up onto the mount of transfiguration; Christ had shown him the glory of heaven in a vision. Now that he should deny Christ after receiving such remarkable love from him, this broke his heart with grief: “he went outside and wept bitterly.”

By this let us test our love to God. Are our hearts spiritual stills, dropping the water of godly tears? Do we grieve for our unkindness against God, our abuse of mercy, our failure to use our talents? How far from loving God are those who sin daily and whose hearts never strike them! They have a sea of sin and not a drop of sorrow. They are so far from being troubled that they make merry with their sins (Jer 11:15): “When you do evil, then you rejoice.” O wretch, did Christ bleed for sin, and do you laugh at it? These are far from loving God. Does a man love his friend when he loves to do him an injury?

4. Another fruit of love is greatness of spirit.88 Love is valiant; it turns cowardice into courage. Love will make a man venture on the greatest difficulties and dangers. Amor nescit difficultates [Love knows no difficulties]. The timid hen will fly at a dog or a snake to defend her young. Love pours μεγαλόψυχον θυμὸν, a spirit of gallantry and fortitude, into a Christian. He who loves God will stand up in his cause and be an advocate for him (Acts 4:20): “We cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard.” He who is afraid to acknowledge Christ has only a little love for him. Nicodemus came sneaking to Christ at night (John 3:2); he was afraid of being seen with him in the daytime. “Love drives out fear.” As the sun drives away fogs and mists, so divine love in great measure drives out carnal fear. Does a man love God when he can hear his blessed truths spoken against and stay silent? He who loves his friend will stand up for him and defend him when he is reviled. Does Christ appear for us in heaven, and are we afraid to appear for him on earth? Love puts heart into a Christian. It fires his heart with zeal and steels it with courage.

5. The fifth fruit of love is tender feeling. If we love God,89 our hearts ache for the dishonors wicked men do to God. We see not only the banks of religion but of common decency broken down, and a flood of wickedness coming in. We see God’s Sabbaths profaned, his oath violated, his name dishonored. If there is any love to God in us, we will take these things to heart. Lot’s righteous soul was “distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless” (2 Pet 2:7). He took the sins of Sodom and made spears of them to pierce his own soul. How far from loving God are those who are not moved at all by his dishonor! If only they have peace and trade, they take nothing to heart. A man who is dead drunk never notices or feels it, though another man is bleeding to death beside him. So many, being drunk with the wine of prosperity, feel nothing when the honor of God is wounded and his truths lie bleeding. If men loved God, they would grieve to see his glory suffer and religion itself become a martyr.

6. The sixth fruit of love is hatred of sin.90 Fire purges the dross from the metal; the fire of love purges out sin. Hos 14:8: “Ephraim shall say, ‘What have I to do anymore with idols?’” He who loves God will have nothing to do with sin, except to give battle to it. Sin is Dei-cidium [the killing of God]; it strikes not only at God’s honor but at his being. Does a man love his prince when he shelters a traitor to the crown? Is he a friend to God who loves what God hates91? The love of God and the love of sin cannot live together. The affections cannot be carried toward two opposites at the same time. A man cannot love health and love poison too, and so one cannot love God and sin too. He who allows any secret sin in his heart is as far from loving God as heaven is from earth.

7. Another fruit of love is crucifixion.92 He who loves God is dead to the world (Gal 6:14): “I have been crucified … to the world.” I am dead to its honors and pleasures. He who is in love with God is not much in love with anything else93. His love to God moves swiftly, like the sun in the sky; but his love to the world is like the motion of the sun on the dial, which is very slow. The love of God and a violent love of the world cannot stand together94 (1 John 2:15): “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.” Love to God swallows up all other love, as Moses’ rod swallowed up the Egyptian rods. If a man could live in the sun, what a small point the whole earth would be! So when a man’s heart is raised above the world in wondering at God and loving him, how poor and slight these things below are! They seem as nothing in his eye. It was a sign that the first Christians loved God that their money did not lie near their hearts: they laid their money at the apostles’ feet (Acts 4:35).

Test your+ love to God by this. What shall we think of those who never have enough of the world? They have the dry dropsy of covetousness, thirsting without end after riches (Amos 2:7): “who pant after the dust of the earth.” Never talk of your+ love to Christ, says Ignatius, ὅταν τὸν κόσμον προτιμᾶτε, when you+ prefer the world to the pearl of great price. And are there not many such, who prize their gold above God? If they have a south land, they do not care for the water of life. They will sell Christ and a good conscience for money. Will God ever give heaven to those who value him so basely, and prefer glittering dust to the glorious Deity? What is there in the earth that we should set our hearts on it so? It is only that the devil makes us look at it through a magnifying glass. The world has no real worth in itself; it is only paint and counterfeit gold. The world has two breasts. The one breast is dry: it is vanity. The other breast runs blood: it is vexation.

8. The next fruit of love is fear.95 In the godly, love and fear kiss each other. Two kinds of fear arise from love.

(1.) A fear of displeasing. The wife loves her husband, and so she will rather deny herself than displease him. The more we love God, the more afraid we are of grieving his Spirit (Gen 39:9): “How could I do such a great evil and sin against God?” When the Empress Eudoxia threatened to banish Chrysostom, he said, “Tell her I fear nothing but sin.” That is a blessed love which puts a Christian into a hot fit of zeal and a cold fit of fear, making him shake and tremble, so that he does not dare willingly to offend God.

(2.) A fear mixed with watchful concern (1 Sam 4:13): Eli’s “heart trembled for the ark of God.” It is not said that his heart trembled for Hophni and Phinehas, his two sons, but for the ark, because if the ark were taken, then “the glory has departed.” He who loves God is full of fear that it may go badly with the church. He fears that profaneness (which is the plague of leprosy) may increase, that popery may get a footing, that God may depart from a people. The presence of God in his ordinances is the beauty and strength of a nation. The Trojans had the image of Pallas, and they believed that as long as that image was kept among them, they would never be conquered. As long as God’s presence is with a people, they are safe. But the soul that is on fire with love to God fears that the visible tokens of God’s presence may be removed.

Let us test our love to God by this touchstone. Many fear that peace and trade may go, but not that God and his gospel may go. Are these lovers of God? He who loves God is more afraid of losing spiritual blessings than earthly ones. If the Sun of righteousness departs from our horizon, what can follow but darkness? What comfort can an organ or an anthem give if the gospel is gone? Is it not like the sound of a trumpet, or a volley of shots, at a funeral?

9. If we are lovers of God, we love what God loves.96

(1.) We love God’s word. David valued the word above honey for its sweetness (Ps 119:103), and above gold for its worth (Ps 119:72). The lines of Scripture are richer than mines of gold. We may well love the word: it is the guiding star that directs us to heaven; it is the field in which the pearl is hidden. The man who does not love the word, but thinks it too strict, and could wish any part of the Bible torn out (as that adulterer did the seventh commandment), does not have the least spark of love in his heart.

(2.) We love God’s day. We do not only keep a Sabbath, but love a Sabbath. Isa 58:13: “If you call the Sabbath a delight.” The Sabbath is what keeps up the face of religion among us; this day must be set apart as glorious to the Lord. The house of God is βασιλικὴ, the palace of the great King. On the Sabbath God shows himself there through the lattice. If we love God, we prize his day above all other days. The whole week would be dark if it were not for this day. On this day manna falls double. Now, if ever, heaven’s gate stands open, and God comes down in a golden shower. On this blessed day the Sun of righteousness rises on the soul. How a gracious heart prizes that day, which was made for the very purpose of enjoying God!

(3.) We love God’s laws. A gracious soul is glad of the law, because it checks his sinful excesses. The heart would be ready to run wild in sin if the law of God did not put some blessed restraints on it. He who loves God loves his law: the law of repentance, the law of self-denial. Many say they love God, but they hate his laws (Ps 2:3): “Let us break Their chains and cast away Their cords.” God’s precepts are compared to cords; they bind men to good behavior. But the wicked think these cords too tight, and so they say, let us break them. They profess to love Christ as a Savior, but hate him as a Prince. Christ tells us of his yoke (Matt 11:29). Sinners would have Christ put a crown on their head, but not a yoke on their neck. He would be a strange king who ruled without laws.

(4.) We love God’s picture; we love his image shining in the saints (1 John 5:1): “Everyone who loves the Father also loves those born of Him.” It is possible to love a saint and yet not love him as a saint. We may love him for something else: for his good nature, or because he is friendly and generous. A beast loves a man, but not quatenus homo, as he is a man; it loves him because he feeds it and gives it fodder. But to love a saint as he is a saint is a sign of love to God. If we love a saint for his saintliness, as having something of God in him, then we love him in these four cases.

[1.] We love a saint though he is poor. A man who loves gold loves a piece of gold though it is wrapped in a rag. So though a saint is in rags, we love him, because there is aliquid Christi, something of Christ, in him.

[2.] We love a saint though he has many personal failings. There is no perfection here. In some, rash anger prevails; in some, inconstancy; in some, too much love of the world. A saint in this life is like gold in the ore: much dross of weakness clings to him, yet we love him for the grace that is in him. A saint is like a fair face with a scar: we love the beautiful face of holiness, though there is a scar on it. The best emerald has its flaws, the brightest stars their twinkling, and the best of the saints their failings. You who cannot love another because of his weaknesses, how would you have God love you? Do you not have plenty of your own?

[3.] We love the saints though they differ from us in some lesser things. Perhaps another Christian does not have as much light as you, and that may make him err in some things. Will you at once unsaint him because he cannot come up to your light?97 Where there is union in fundamentals, there ought to be union in affections.

[4.] We love the saints though they are persecuted. We love precious metal though it is in the furnace. Paul bore in his body the marks of the Lord Jesus (Gal 6:17). Those marks were like the soldier’s scar, honorable. We must love a saint in chains as well as in scarlet. Constantine kissed the empty socket of Paphnutius’ eye, because he had lost his eye for Christ. If we love Christ, we love his persecuted members.

If this is loving God, to love his image sparkling in the saints, oh, then how few lovers of God are to be found! Do they love God who hate those who are like God? Do they love Christ’s person who are filled with a spirit of revenge against his people? How can a wife be said to love her husband when she tears up his picture? Surely Judas and Julian are not dead yet; their spirit lives in the world. Who are guilty but the innocent? What greater crime is there than holiness, if the devil may sit on the grand jury? Wicked men seem to show great reverence to the saints who have died. They canonize dead saints, but persecute living ones. In vain do men stand up at the Creed and tell the world that they “believe in God,” when they loathe one of the articles of the Creed, namely, “the communion of saints.” Surely there is no greater sign that a man is ripe for hell than this: not only to lack grace, but to hate it.

10. Another blessed sign of love is to have good thoughts of God. He who loves his friend takes what his friend does in the best sense. 1 Cor 13:5: “Love thinks no evil.” Malice interprets everything in the worst sense; love interprets everything in the best sense. It is an excellent commentator on providence; “it thinks no evil.” He who loves God has a good opinion of God. Though God afflicts sharply, the soul takes it all well. This is the language of a gracious spirit: “My God sees what a hard heart I have, and so he drives in one wedge of affliction after another to break my heart. He knows how full I am of infection, how sick with pleurisy, and so he bleeds me to save my life. This severe dealing is either to mortify some corruption or to exercise some grace. How good God is, that he will not leave me alone in my sins, but strikes my body to save my soul!” So he who loves God takes everything in good part. Love puts a fair interpretation on all God’s actions. You who are inclined to murmur against God, as if he had dealt badly with you, be humbled for this. Say to yourself, “If I loved God more, I would have better thoughts of God.” It is Satan who makes us have good thoughts of ourselves and hard thoughts of God. Love takes everything in the fairest sense; “it thinks no evil.”

11. The eleventh fruit of love is obedience (John 14:21): “Whoever has My commandments and keeps them98 is the one who loves Me.” Pater adsum, impera quid vis99 [Father, here I am; command what you will]. It is a vain thing to say we love Christ’s person if we slight his commands. Does that child love his father who refuses to obey him100? If we love God, we will obey him in those things that cross flesh and blood:

  1. In things that are difficult.
  2. In things that are dangerous.

(1.) In things that are difficult. As: (1) In mortifying sin. There are some sins that are not only near to us as our clothes, but dear to us as our eye. If we love God, we will set ourselves against these, both in purpose and in practice. (2) In forgiving our enemies. God commands us on pain of death to forgive (Eph 4:32): “forgiving each other”101. This is hard; it is going against the stream. We are apt to forget kindnesses and remember injuries. But if we love God, we will pass over offenses. When we seriously consider how many talents God has forgiven us, and how many affronts and insults he has put up with from us, it makes us copy his example and try to bury an injury rather than pay it back.

(2.) In things that are dangerous. When God calls us to suffer for him, we will obey. Love made Christ suffer for us; love was the chain that fastened him to the cross. So if we love God, we will be willing to suffer for him. Love has a strange quality: it is the least suffering grace, and yet it is the most suffering grace. It is the least suffering grace in one sense: it will not allow known sin to lie in the soul unrepented of, and it will not allow abuses and dishonors to be done to God. In this way it is the least suffering grace. Yet it is the most suffering grace: it will suffer reproaches, chains, and imprisonment for Christ’s sake (Acts 21:13): “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die … for the name of the Lord Jesus.” It is true that not every Christian is a martyr, but he has a spirit of martyrdom in him. He says with Paul, “ἑτοίμως ἔχω, I am ready … to be bound.” He has a disposition of mind to suffer, if God calls. Love will carry men beyond their own strength. Tertullian observes how much the heathen suffered for love of their country: Vicit amor patriae [love of country won]. If the spring of nature rises so high, surely grace will rise higher. If love of their country will make men suffer, much more should love to Christ. 1 Cor 13:7: “Love … endures all things.” Basil tells of a virgin condemned to the fire. She was offered her life and her property if she would bow down to the idol, and she answered, “Let life and money go; welcome Christ”102. It was a noble and zealous saying of Ignatius: “Let me be ground by the teeth of wild beasts, if only I may be God’s pure wheat”103. How divine affection carried the first saints above the love of life and the fear of death! Stephen was stoned, Luke hanged on an olive tree, Peter crucified at Jerusalem with his head downward104. These divine heroes were willing to suffer rather than make the name of God suffer by their cowardice. How Paul rattled the chain he wore for Christ105! He gloried in it ὡς γύνη φιλόκοσμος, like a woman who is proud of her jewels, says Chrysostom. And holy Ignatius wore his fetters like a bracelet of diamonds. Heb 11:35: “Others … refused their release.” They refused to come out of prison on sinful terms; they preferred their innocence to their liberty.

Let us test our love to God by this: do we have a spirit of martyrdom? Many say they love God, but how does it show? They will not give up the least comfort or bear the least cross for his sake. Suppose Jesus Christ had said to us, “I love you+ well, you+ are dear to me, but I cannot suffer; I cannot lay down my life for you+.” We would have questioned his love very much. And might not Christ suspect us, when we profess love to him and yet will endure nothing for him? Those who bear true affection to God will, according to their vow in baptism, fight under his banner to the death, and make Christ’s crown flourish in their ashes.

12. He who loves God will try to make him appear glorious in the eyes of others.106 Those who are in love will be praising and setting forth the loveliness of the persons they love. The love-sick bride describes Christ in all his beauty (Song 5:11, 13): “His head is purest gold … His cheeks are like beds of spice.” If we love God, we will spread abroad his excellencies, so that we may raise his fame and esteem and draw others to fall in love with him. Love cannot be silent. We will be so many trumpets, sounding out the freeness of God’s grace, the surpassing greatness of his love, and the glory of his kingdom. Love is like fire: where it burns in the heart, it will break out at the lips. It will be eloquent and moving in setting forth God’s praise. Love must have a vent.

13. The thirteenth fruit of love is107 to long for Christ’s appearing. 2 Tim 4:8: “From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness … and not only to me, but to all who love His appearing.” Love desires union, and Aristotle gives the reason: because joy flows from union. When our union with Christ is perfect in glory, then our joy will be full. He who loves Christ loves his appearing. Christ’s appearing will be a happy appearing for the saints. His appearing now, when he appears for us as an advocate (Heb 9:24), is a great comfort. But the other appearing will be infinitely more, when he appears for us as our husband. On that day he will give us two jewels. (1) His love: a love so great and astonishing that it is better felt than expressed. (2) His likeness (1 John 3:2): “When Christ appears, we will be like Him.” And from both of these, love and likeness, infinite joy will flow into the soul. No wonder, then, that he who loves Christ longs for his appearing. Does not the bride long for the wedding day? “The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’ … Come, Lord Jesus!” (Rev 22:17). Let us test our love to Christ by this. A wicked man, who is αὐτοκατάκριτος, self-condemned, is afraid of Christ’s appearing; he wishes he would never appear. But those who love Christ are joyful to think of his coming in the clouds. Then they will be delivered from all their sins and fears; they will be acquitted before men and angels, and will be carried forever into the paradise of God.

14. Love will make us stoop to the lowliest tasks.108 Love is a humble grace. It does not walk about in pomp; it will creep on its hands. It will stoop and submit to anything by which it may be of service to Christ. We see this in Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus. Both of them were men of honor, yet one takes down Christ’s body with his own hands, and the other embalms it with sweet spices. It might seem a great deal for persons of their rank to be employed in that service, but love made them do it. If we love God, we will not think any work too lowly for us in which we may be of help to Christ’s members. Love is not squeamish. It will visit the sick, relieve the poor, and wash the saints’ wounds. The mother who loves her child is not fussy or dainty; she will do things for her child that others would scorn to do. He who loves God will humble himself to the lowliest task of love to Christ and his members. These are the fruits of love to God. Happy are those who can find these fruits of another country growing in their souls.
