Chapter X

An exhortation to love God.

Use 3. The third use is one of exhortation,109 and it has three branches. 1. Let me earnestly persuade all who bear the name of Christians to become lovers of God (Ps 31:23):110 “Love the Lord, all His saints.” There are only a few who love God. Many give him a hypocritical kiss, but few love him. It is not as easy to love God as most imagine. The affection of love is natural, but the grace is not. By nature men are θεοστυγεῖς, God-haters (Rom 1:30). The wicked would flee from God; they would be neither under his rules nor within his reach. They fear God, but they do not love him. All the strength in men or angels cannot make the heart love God. Ordinances will not do it of themselves, nor will judgments. Only the almighty and invincible power of the Spirit of God can pour love into the soul. Since this is so hard a work, it calls on us all the more to pray and labor earnestly for this angelic grace of love111. To stir up and kindle our desires for it, I will set down twenty motives.

Motives to Love God

1. Without this, all our religion is vain. It is not duty, but love to duty, that God looks at; it is not how much we do,112 but how much we love. If a servant does not do his work willingly and out of love, it is not accepted. Duties not mixed with love are as burdensome to God as they are to us. That is why David counsels his son Solomon to serve God with a willing mind (1 Chr 28:9). To do duty without love is not sacrifice but penance.

2. Love is the most noble and excellent grace. It is a pure flame kindled from heaven. By it we resemble God, who is love. Believing and obeying do not make us like God, but by love we grow like him (1 John 4:16). Love is the grace that most delights in God, and it is most delightful to him. The disciple who was most full of love lay on Christ’s bosom. Love puts freshness and luster on all the graces; the graces seem to be eclipsed unless love shines and sparkles in them. Faith is not true unless it is “working through love.” The waters of repentance are not pure unless they flow from the spring of love. Love is the savory food God loves. It is the incense that makes all our services sweet and fragrant. It is vinum aromaticum, “the spiced wine” and “the nectar of the pomegranate.”

3. Is anything God requires unreasonable? It is only our love. If he asked for our property, or for the fruit of our bodies, could we deny him? But he asks only for our love. He would only pick this flower. Is this a hard request? Was there ever a debt so easily paid as this? We do not make ourselves poorer at all by paying it. Love is no burden. Is it any labor for the bride to love her husband? Love is delightful: Non potest amor esse, et dulcis non esse113 [Love cannot be, and not be sweet].

4. God is the most fully suited and complete object of our love. All the excellencies that lie scattered among created things are twisted together and united in him. He is a storehouse of blessings. He is wisdom, beauty, love; indeed, the very essence of goodness. He is Optimus Maximus [the best and greatest]. There is nothing in God that can cause disgust or loathing. Created things sooner surfeit than satisfy, but fresh beauties keep sparkling forth in God; the more we enjoy of him, the more we are enraptured with delight.

There is nothing in God to dull our affections or quench our love: no weakness, no deformity, such as usually weaken and cool love. There is such a delicious sweetness in God that it may not only entice but command our love. Suppose there were more angels in heaven than there are, and all those glorious seraphim had an immense flame of love burning in their breasts to eternity. Still they could not love God in a measure equal to the infinite perfection and surpassing goodness that is in him. Surely, then, here is enough to draw us to fall in love with God. We cannot spend our love on a better object.

5. Love makes religion easy. It oils the wheels of the affections and makes them more lively and cheerful in God’s service. Love takes away the tediousness of duty. Jacob thought seven years only a little, for the love he had for Rachel. Love makes duty a pleasure. Why are the angels so swift and winged in God’s service? It is because they love him. Love is never weary. He who loves gold is never weary of counting it, and he who loves God is never weary of serving him.

6. God desires our love. It would be a great thing for a king to desire the love of a woman who was deformed and leprous. We have lost our beauty and stained our blood, yet the King of heaven is a suitor to us. What is there in our love that God should come wooing for it? How is God any better for our love? He does not need it; he is infinitely blessed in himself. If we deny him our love, he has higher creatures who pay him the cheerful tribute of love. God does not need our love, yet he seeks it.

7. God has deserved our love. How he has loved us! Our affections should be kindled at the fire of God’s love. What a miracle of love it is that God should love us when there was nothing lovely in us! Ezek 16:6: “As you lay there in your blood I said to you, ‘Live!’” The time of our loathsomeness was the time of God’s love. We had something in us to provoke fury, but nothing to attract love. What a surpassing love it was to give Christ to us114! That Christ should die for sinners: God has set all the angels in heaven wondering at this love. Augustine says, “The cross was a pulpit, and the lesson Christ preached on it was love.” O the living love of a dying Savior! Per vulnera viscera [through the wounds, the heart]. I think I see Christ on the cross, bleeding all over. I think I hear him say to us, “Reach your+ hands here; put them into my side; feel my bleeding heart, and see whether I do not love you+. And will you+ not give your+ love to me? Will you+ love the world more than me? Did the world appease the wrath of God for you+? Have I not done all this? And will you+ not love me?” It is natural to love where we are loved. Christ has set us a copy of love and written it in his blood; let us labor to write after so fair a copy and imitate him in love.

8. Love to God is the best self-love. It is self-love to get the soul saved, and by loving God we advance our own salvation. 1 John 4:16: “Whoever dwells in love dwells in God, and God in him.” And he who has God dwelling in his heart is sure to dwell with God in heaven. So to love God is the truest self-love; he who does not love God does not love himself.

9. Love to God is evidence of sincerity (Song 1:4): “The upright love you.” Many a child of God fears he is a hypocrite. Do you love God? When Peter was downcast in the sense of his sin, he thought himself unworthy that Christ should ever take notice of him, or employ him any more in the work of his apostleship. See how Christ sets about comforting him (John 21:15): “Simon son of John, do you love Me …?” It is as if Christ had said, “Though you have denied me through fear, yet if you can say from your heart that you love me, you are sincere and upright.” To love God is a better sign of sincerity than to fear him. The Israelites feared God’s justice (Ps 78:34): “When He slew them, they would seek Him; they repented and searched for God.” But what did it all come to? (vv. 36, 37): “But they flattered Him with their mouths, and lied to Him with their tongues. Their hearts were disloyal to Him.” That repentance is no better than flattery which arises only from fear of God’s judgments and has no love mixed with it. Loving God is evidence that God has the heart; and if the heart is his, it will command all the rest.

10. By our love to God we may conclude God’s love to us (1 John 4:19): “We love Him because He first loved us.” “Oh,” says the soul, “if I knew God loved me, I could rejoice.” Do you love God? Then you may be sure of God’s love to you. It is as with burning glasses: if the glass burns, it is because the sun has first shone on it; otherwise it could not burn. So if our hearts burn in love to God, it is because God’s love has first shone on us; otherwise we could not burn in love. Our love is nothing but the reflection of God’s love.

11. If you+ do not love God, you+ will love something else, either the world or sin. And are these worthy of your+ love? Is it not better to love God than these?

1. First, it is better to love God than the world, as appears in these eight particulars.

(1.) If you+ set your+ love on worldly things, they will not satisfy. You+ may as well satisfy your+ body with air as your+ soul with earth (Eccl 5:10). Job 20:22: “In the midst of his plenty, he will be distressed.” Plenty has its poverty. If the globe of the world were yours+, it would not fill you+. Adam had two sons, Cain and Abel. Cain means possession; Abel means vanity. This shows us that in all our possessions there is vanity. And will you+ set your+ love on what will never give you+ contentment? Is it not better to love God? He will give you+ what will satisfy (Ps 17:15): “When I awake, I will be satisfied with Your likeness.” When I awake out of the sleep of death, and some of the rays and beams of God’s glory are put on me, then I will be satisfied with his likeness.

(2.) If you+ love worldly things, they cannot remove trouble of mind. If a thorn has got into the conscience, all the world cannot pluck it out. When King Saul was troubled in mind, all his crown jewels could not comfort him (1 Sam 28:15). But if you+ love God, he can give you+ peace when nothing else can115. He can turn “darkness into dawn” (Amos 5:8). He can drop in Christ’s blood, which is a cooling drink. He can whisper his love by the Spirit and with one smile scatter all your+ fears and unrest.

(3.) If you+ love the world, you+ may love what may hinder you+ from heaven. Worldly comforts may be compared to the wagons of an army: while the soldiers have been getting provisions from the wagons, they have lost the battle. Mark 10:23: “How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God!” Prosperity is to many like a sail to a boat, which quickly overturns it. So by loving the world you+ may love what will endanger you+116. But if you+ love God, there is no fear of losing heaven. He will be a rock to hide you+, not to hurt you+. By loving him we come to enjoy him.

(4.) You+ may love worldly things, and they cannot love you+ back. You+ love gold and silver, but your+ gold cannot love you+ back. You+ love a picture, but the picture cannot love you+ back. You+ give your+ love away to created things and receive no love in return. But if you+ love God, he will love you+ back (John 14:23): “If anyone loves Me … My Father will love him, and We will come to him and make Our home with him.” God will not be behind us in love; for our drop we will receive an ocean.

(5.) When you+ love the world, you+ love what is worse than yourselves+. The soul (as John of Damascus says) is a spark of heavenly brightness; it carries in it an idea and likeness of God. While you+ love the world, you+ love what is infinitely below the worth of your+ souls. Will anyone spend money on sackcloth? When you lay out your love on the world, you lay out gold on dung; you hang a pearl on a pig; you love what is lower than yourself. Christ speaks of the birds of the air in another sense (Matt 6:26): “Are you+ not much better than they?” So I say of worldly things, “Are you+ not much better than they?” You+ love a fine house, a beautiful picture; are you+ not much better than they? But if you+ love God, you+ now place your+ love on the most noble and exalted object; you+ love what is better than yourselves+. God is better than the soul, better than angels, better than heaven.

(6.) You+ may love the world and have hatred in return for your+ love (John 15:19): “The world hates you+, because you+ are not of the world.” Would it not vex a man to spend money on a piece of ground, and then, instead of bringing forth grain or grapes, it yielded nothing but nettles? So it is with all things under the moon: we love them, and they prove to be nettles that sting. The world is a stepmother: instead of giving the breast, it draws the sword. We meet with nothing but either disappointment or unkindness (Judg 9:15): “May fire come out of the thornbush and consume the cedars of Lebanon.” While we love created things, fire comes out of this thornbush to devour us. But if we love God, he will not return hatred for love (Prov 8:17): “I love those who love me.” God may chastise, but he cannot hate. Every believer is part of Christ, and God could as soon hate Christ as hate a believer.

(7.) You+ may love created things too much. You+ may love wine too much, silver too much, but you+ cannot love God too much. If it were possible to go too far, excess here would be a virtue. But our sin is that we cannot love God enough (Ezek 16:30): “How weak is your heart!” So it may be said, how weak is our love to God! It is like the water of the last drawing from the still, which has less spirit in it. If we could love God far more than we do, it would still not be in proportion to his worth. So there is no danger of excess in our love to God.

(8.) You+ may love worldly things, and they die and leave you+. Riches take wings; relatives drop away117. The Romans painted the vanity of worldly things in the form of a man: in his right hand a rose, in his left hand a lily, under his feet wormwood. It is an emblem of the world. The rose is sweet and the lily fair, but both are fading; and under the feet is wormwood: at death all the delights of the world will be bitter. There is nothing here that lasts118. Every created thing has a little honey in its mouth, but it has wings; it will soon fly away. Vitae primordium, mortis prodromum [the beginning of life is the forerunner of death]. But if you+ love God, he is a portion forever (Ps 73:26). As he is called a sun for comfort, so he is called a rock for eternity; he abides forever. So we see it is better to love God than the world.

(2.) Secondly, it is better to love God than sin. What is there in sin that anyone should love it119? (1) Sin is a debt: “Forgive us our debts.” It is a debt that binds us over to the wrath of God. Why should we love sin? Does any man love to be in debt? (2) Sin is a disease (Isa 1:5): “The whole head is sick.” And will you love sin? Will any man hug a disease? Will he love his plague-sores? (3) Sin is a pollution. The apostle calls it ῥυπαρία, filthiness (Jas 1:21). It is compared to leprosy, to the poison of asps, to vomit. God’s heart rises against sinners (Zech 11:8): “My soul loathed them.” Sin is a misshapen monster. Lust makes a man brutish; malice makes him devilish. What is there in sin to be loved? Shall we love deformity? (4) Sin is an enemy. It is compared to a serpent (Prov 23:32). It has four stings: shame, guilt, horror, death. Will a man love what seeks his death? Surely, then, it is better to love God than sin120. God will save you; sin will damn you. Is not he bewitched who loves damnation?

12. The relation we stand in to God calls for love. There is a close bond of marriage (Isa 54:5): “Your husband is your Maker.” And shall not a wife love her husband? He is full of tenderness. His bride is to him as the apple of his eye; he rejoices over her as the bridegroom over the bride (Isa 62:5). He loves the believer as he loves Christ (John 17:26), with the same love in quality, though not in equality. If God is a husband, shall we not love him? The bond calls for affection. Either we must love God, or we give ground to suspect that we are not yet married to him.

13. Love is the most lasting grace. It will stay with us when the other graces take their leave. In heaven we will need no repentance, because we will have no sin. In heaven we will not need patience, because there will be no affliction. In heaven there will be no need of faith. Faith looks at things unseen (Heb 11:1), but then we will see God face to face; and where there is sight, there is no need of faith.

But when the other graces are out of date, love continues. In this sense the apostle says love is greater than faith, because it lasts longest (1 Cor 13:8): οὐδέποτε ἐκπίπτει, “Love never fails.” Faith is the Jacob’s staff we walk with in this life (2 Cor 5:7): “We walk by faith.” But we will set this Jacob’s staff down at heaven’s door, and only love will enter. So love carries away the crown from all the other graces. Love is the longest-lived grace; it is a blossom of eternity. How we should strive to excel in this grace, which alone will live with us in heaven and accompany us to the marriage supper of the Lamb!

14. Love to God will never let sin thrive in the heart. Some plants will not thrive when they are close together, like the laurel and the vine. The love of God withers sin. Though the old man lives, he is like a sick man: he is weak, and his breath is short. Love, like the water of jealousy, makes the thigh of sin rot. The flower of love kills the weed of sin. Though sin does not die completely, it dies daily. How we should labor for that grace, which is the only aqua fortis [strong acid] to destroy sin!

15. Love to God is an excellent means for growth in grace (2 Pet 3:18): “But grow in the grace.” Growth in grace is very pleasing to God. Christ accepts the truth of grace, but commends the degrees of grace. And what can promote and increase grace more than love to God? Love is like watering the root, which makes the tree grow. That is why the apostle uses this expression in his prayer (2 Thess 3:5): “May the Lord direct your+ hearts into the love of God.” He knew that this grace of love would nurse and cherish all the graces.

16. Consider the great benefit that will come to us if we love God (1 Cor 2:9): “No eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him.” The eye has seen rare sights; the ear has heard sweet music. “But no eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him!” Such glorious rewards are laid up that (as Augustine says) faith itself is not able to grasp them. God has promised a crown of life to those who love him (Jas 1:12). This crown encircles within it all blessedness, riches, glory, and delight, and it is a crown that never fades away (1 Pet 5:4). In this way God would bribe us to love him by rewards.

17. Love to God is armor proof against error. For lack of hearts full of love, men have heads full of error. Unholy opinions come from the lack of holy affections. Why are men given up to “a powerful delusion,” except that “they refused the love of the truth” (2 Thess 2:10, 11)? The more we love God, the more we hate those unorthodox opinions that would draw us away from God into libertinism. The more a man loves health, the more he hates mercury.

18. If we love God, we have all winds blowing for us; everything in the world will conspire for our good. We do not know what fiery trials we may meet with, but for those who love God all things will work for good. The things that work against them will work for them. Their cross will make way for a crown; every wind will blow them to the heavenly port.

19. Lack of love to God is the root of apostasy. The seed in the parable that had no root fell away. He who does not have the love of God rooted in his heart will fall away in time of temptation. He who loves God will cling to him as Ruth clung to Naomi (Ruth 1:16): “Wherever you go, I will go … Where you die, I will die.” But he who lacks love to God will do as Orpah did to her mother-in-law: she kissed her and said goodbye to her. A soldier who has no love for his commander will leave him when he sees an opportunity and run over to the enemy’s side. He who has no love to God in his heart, you may mark down as an apostate.

20. Love is the only thing in which we can repay God in kind. If God is angry with us, we must not be angry in return. If he rebukes us, we must not rebuke him in return. But if God loves us, we must love him in return. There is nothing in which we can answer God in kind but love. We must not give him word for word, but we must give him love for love. So we have seen twenty motives to stir up and kindle our love to God.

The Means of Love

Question. How shall we come to love God?

Answer. 1. Study God. If we studied him more, we would love him more. Take a view of his surpassing excellencies121: his holiness, his incomprehensible goodness. The angels know God better than we do and clearly see the splendor of his majesty, and that is why they are so deeply in love with him.

2. Labor to have God for your own (Ps 63:1): “O God, You are my God.” That pronoun my is suavissima amoris illecebra, a sweet magnet to love; a man loves what is his own. The more we believe, the more we love. Faith is the root, and love is the flower that grows on it (Gal 5:6): “faith, working through love.”

3. Make it your+ earnest request to God that he will give you+ a heart to love him.122 This is an acceptable request; surely God will not deny it. King Solomon asked God for wisdom (1 Kgs 3:9): “Give Your servant an understanding heart.” Verse 10: “It pleased the Lord.” So when you cry to God, “Lord, give me a heart to love you; it is my grief that I cannot love you more; O kindle this fire from heaven on the altar of my heart,” surely this prayer pleases the Lord, and he will pour out his Spirit on you, whose golden oil will make the lamp of your love burn bright.

Preserving Love from a Consumption

2. I proceed to the second branch of the exhortation. You+ who have love to God, labor to preserve it; do not let this love die and be quenched123. As you+ would have God’s love continued to you+, let your+ love be continued to him. Love, like fire, will be ready to go out (Rev 2:4): “You have abandoned your first love.” Satan labors to blow out this flame, and through neglect of duty we lose it. When a delicate body leaves off its clothes, it is apt to catch cold. So when we leave off duty, we cool by degrees in our love to God. Of all the graces, love is the quickest to decay; so we need to be all the more careful to preserve it. If a man has a jewel, he will keep it; if he has land by inheritance, he will keep it. How careful, then, should we be to keep this grace of love? It is sad to see professing Christians declining in their love to God. Many are in a spiritual consumption; their love is wasting away.

There are four signs by which Christians may know that their love is in a consumption.

(1.) When they have lost their taste. He who is far gone in a consumption has no taste; he does not find the same savory relish in his food as before. So when Christians have lost their taste and find no sweetness in a promise, it is a sign of a spiritual consumption (1 Pet 2:3): “now that you+ have tasted that the Lord is good.” There was a time when they found comfort in drawing near to God. His word was like dripping honey, very delicious to the palate of their soul. But now it is otherwise: they can taste no more sweetness in spiritual things than in “the white of an egg” (Job 6:6). This is a sign that they are in a consumption. To lose the taste shows the loss of the first love.

(2.) When Christians have lost their appetite. A man far gone in a consumption does not have the same stomach for his food as before. There was a time when Christians did hunger and thirst for righteousness. They cared for things of a heavenly kind: the grace of the Spirit, the blood of the cross, the light of God’s face. They had a stomach for ordinances and came to them like a hungry man to a feast. But now the case is altered. They have no appetite; they do not prize Christ as they did; they do not have such strong affections for the word; their hearts are not burning within them. It is a sad sign that they are in a consumption and their love is wasting away. It was a sign that David’s natural strength had failed when they covered him with clothes and yet he got no heat (1 Kgs 1:1). So when men are plied with hot clothes, I mean ordinances, yet have no heat of affection, but are cold and stiff, as if they were ready to be laid out for burial, it is a sign that their first love has declined. They are far gone in a consumption.

(3.) When Christians grow more in love with the world, it shows a decrease of spiritual love. They were once of an exalted, heavenly temper; they spoke the language of Canaan. But now they are like the fish in the gospel that had money in its mouth (Matt 17:27). They cannot utter three words without one of them being about Mammon. Their thoughts and affections (like Satan) are always roaming through the earth. It is a sign that they are going quickly downhill; their love to God is in a consumption. We may observe that when nature decays and grows weaker, people walk more stooped. And truly, when the heart stoops more to the earth, and is so bent over that it can hardly lift itself up to a heavenly thought, it is now sadly declining in its first love. When rust clings to metal, it not only takes away the metal’s brightness, but eats into it and consumes it. So when the earth clings to men’s souls, it not only dims the shining luster of their graces, but by degrees eats away their graces.

(4.) When Christians make little account of the worship of God. They perform the duties of religion in a dead, formal manner. If the duties are not left undone, they are badly done. This is a sad symptom of a spiritual consumption; slackness in duty shows a decay in our first love. When the strings of a viol are slack, the viol can never make good music. When men grow slack in duty, they pray as if they did not pray, and this can never make any harmonious sound in God’s ears. When the spiritual motion, like that of the eighth sphere, is slow and heavy, and the pulse of the soul beats low, it is a sign that Christians have abandoned their first love.

Let us beware of this spiritual consumption. It is dangerous to slacken in our love. Love is a grace we do not know how to do without. A soldier may as well be without his weapons, a painter without his brush, a musician without his viol, as a Christian be without love. The body cannot do without its natural heat. Love is to the soul what natural heat is to the body; there is no living without it. Love moves the graces, stirs up the affections, makes us grieve for sin, and makes us cheerful in God. It is like oil to the wheels; it enlivens us in God’s service. How careful, then, we should be to keep divine love alive!

Question. How may we keep our love from going out?

Answer. Watch your+ hearts every day. Take notice of the first declines in grace. Observe yourselves+ when you+ begin to grow dull and listless, and use every means of quickening. Be much in prayer, meditation, and holy conversation. When the fire is going out, you+ throw on fuel. So when the flame of your+ love is going out, make use of ordinances and gospel promises as fuel to keep the fire of your+ love burning.

Increasing Love to God

3. Let me exhort Christians to increase in love to God. Let your+ love be boiled up higher (Phil 1:9)124: “And this is my prayer: that your+ love may abound μᾶλλον καὶ μᾶλλον, more and more.” Our love to God should be like the light of the morning. First there is the crepusculum, or daybreak; then it shines brighter until full noon. Those who have a few sparks of love should ἀναζωπυρεῖν, blow up those divine sparks into a flame. A Christian should not be content with so small a dram of grace that it makes him doubt whether he has any grace or not. He should keep on increasing the stock. He who has a little gold would like more; you+ who love God a little, labor to love him more. A godly man is like a man with dropsy: the more grace he drinks in, the more he thirsts. He is content with very little of the world, yet he is never satisfied, but would have more of the Spirit’s influence, and labors to add one degree of love to another. To persuade Christians to put more oil in the lamp and increase the flame of their love, let me set before them these four divine incentives.

(1.) The growth of love is evidence of its truth. If I see the almond tree bud and flourish, I know there is life in the root. Paint will not grow; a hypocrite, who is only a picture, will not grow. But where we see love to God increasing and growing bigger (like Elijah’s cloud), we may conclude that it is true and genuine.

(2.) By the growth of love we imitate the saints in the Bible. Their love to God, like the waters of the sanctuary, rose higher. The disciples’ love to Christ was weak at first: they fled from Christ. But after Christ’s death it grew more vigorous, and they openly professed him. Peter’s love was weaker and more feeble at first; he denied Christ. But afterward, how boldly he preached him (Acts 4:10)! Indeed, when Christ put Peter’s love to the test (John 21:16), “Simon son of John, do you love Me?”, Peter could make his humble yet confident appeal to Christ: “Yes, Lord … You know I love You.” So that tender plant, which before was blown down by the wind of a temptation, has now grown into a cedar that all the powers of hell could not shake.

The growth of love will enlarge the reward. The more we burn in love, the more we will shine in glory. The higher our love, the heavier our crown.

(4.) The more we love God, the more love we will have from him. Would we have God open to us the sweet secrets of his love? Would we have the smiles of his face, the kisses of his lips? Oh, then let us strive for higher degrees of love. Paul counted gold and pearls as dung compared with Christ (Phil 3:8). Indeed, he was so on fire with love to God that he could have wished himself cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of his brothers the Jews (Rom 9:3). Not that he could be cut off from Christ; but such was his fervent love and godly zeal for the glory of God that he would have been content to suffer, even beyond what is fit to speak of, if God might have more honor.

Here was love screwed up to the highest pitch that a mortal could possibly reach. And see how near he lay to God’s heart! The Lord makes known to him the arcana coeli [the secrets of heaven]. He takes him up to heaven for a while and lays him in his bosom, where he had such a glorious sight of God and heard those ἄρρητα ῥήματα, “things too sacred for words, things that man is not permitted to tell” (2 Cor 12:4). No man was ever a loser by his love to God.

(5.) If our love to God does not increase, it will soon decrease. If the fire is not blown up, it will quickly go out. So Christians should above all things try to cherish and stir up their love to God. This exhortation will be out of date when we come to heaven, for then our light will be clear and our love perfect. But now it is in season to exhort that our love to God may abound more and more.

Effectual Calling

Chapter XI

Concerning effectual calling.

The second qualification of the persons to whom this privilege in the text belongs is that they are the called of God: all things work together for good τοῖς κλητοῖς, “to those who are called.” Though this word [called] is placed after loving God in order, yet in nature it comes before it. Love is named first, but it is not produced first. We must be called by God before we can love God.

In verse 30 of this chapter, calling is made the middle link of the golden chain of salvation. It is placed between predestination and glorification; and if we hold this middle link fast, we are sure of the two ends of the chain. To make this clearer, six things are to be observed.

Section I. A Distinction about Calling.

1. I will set down a distinction. There are two kinds of call.

(1.) An outward call, which is nothing else than God’s blessed offer of grace in the gospel, his pleading with sinners, when he woos them to come in and accept mercy. Our Savior speaks of this in Matt 20:16: “Many are called, but few are chosen.” This outward call is not enough for salvation, yet it is enough to leave men without excuse.

(2.) There is an inward call, when God wonderfully overpowers the heart and draws the will to embrace Christ. This is, as Augustine puts it, vocatio alta, & efficax, an effectual call. By the outward call God blows a trumpet in the ear; by the inward call he opens the heart, as he opened the heart of Lydia (Acts 16:14). The outward call may bring men to a profession of Christ; the inward call brings them to a possession of Christ. The outward call curbs a sinner; the inward call changes him.

Section II. Our Pitiful Condition before We Are Called.

2.What we are before this call. (1) We are in a state of slavery.125 Before God calls a man, he is at the devil’s call. If the devil says go, he goes. The deluded sinner is like the slave who digs in the mine, cuts stone in the quarry, and pulls at the oar. He is at the command of Satan as the donkey is at the command of the driver. (2) We are in a state of darkness (Eph 5:8): “You+ were once darkness.” First, darkness is very cheerless. A man in the dark is full of fear; he trembles at every step he takes. Second, it is dangerous. He who is in the dark may quickly go out of the right way and fall into rivers and whirlpools. So in the darkness of ignorance we may quickly fall into the whirlpool of hell. (3) Before we are savingly called, we are in a state of helplessness (Rom 5:6): ἡμῶν ἀσθενῶν, “while we were still powerless.” We have no strength to resist a temptation or to grapple with a corruption; sin cut the lock where our strength lay. Indeed, there is not only helplessness but stubbornness (Acts 7:51): “You+ always resist the Holy Spirit.” Besides an unwillingness to do good, there is opposition to it. (4) We are in a state of pollution (Ezek 16:6): “I … saw you polluted in your blood.” The imagination coins earthly thoughts; the heart is the devil’s forge, where the sparks of lust fly. (5) We are in a state of damnation. We are born under a sad planet (John 3:36): “The wrath of God remains on us.” This is our condition before God is pleased by a merciful call to bring us near to himself and free us from the misery in which we were swallowed up before.

Section III. The Means of Our Blessed Call.

3. The means of our effectual call. The ordinary means the Lord uses in calling us is not raptures and revelations, as the Familists hold, but is:

(1.) Partly by his word, which is virga virtutis, the rod of his strength (Ps 110:2). The voice of the word is God’s call to us. That is why he is said to speak to us [now] from heaven (Heb 12:25), that is, in the ministry of the word. When the word calls us from sin, it is as if we heard a voice from heaven.

(2.) Partly by his Spirit; this is the loud call. The word is the instrumental cause of our conversion; the Spirit is the efficient cause. The ministers of God are only the pipes and organs. It is the Spirit blowing in them that effectually changes the heart (Acts 10:44): “While Peter was still speaking …, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard his message”126. It is not the farmer’s hard work in plowing and sowing that will make the ground fruitful without the early and the latter rain. So the seed of the word will not effectually convert unless the Spirit puts forth his sweet influence and drops like rain on the heart. That is why we must pray for the help of God’s Spirit, that he would put forth his powerful voice and wake us out of the grave of unbelief. If a man knocks at a gate of brass, it will not open; but if he comes with a key in his hand, it will open. So when God, who has the key of David in his hand127, comes, he opens the heart, however tightly it is locked against him.

Section IV. God’s Method in Calling Sinners.

4. The method God uses in calling sinners. The Lord does not tie himself to one way, or use the same order with everyone. He comes:

(1.) Sometimes in the still voice. Those who have had godly parents and have sat under the warm sunshine of a religious upbringing often do not know how or when they were called. The Lord secretly and gradually put grace into their hearts, as the dew falls in drops without being felt. They know by the heavenly effects that they are called, but they do not know the time or the manner. The hand moves on the dial, but we do not notice when it moves. This is how God deals with some.

(2.) Others are more stubborn and knotty sinners, and God comes to them in a rough wind. He uses more wedges of the law to break their hearts. He humbles them deeply and shows them they are damned without Christ. Then, having plowed up the fallow ground of their hearts by humbling them, he sows the seeds of comfort. He sets Christ and mercy before them, and draws their wills not only to accept Christ, but to long for him passionately and to rest on him in trust. This is how he worked on Paul, and called him from a persecutor to a preacher. This call is more visible than the other, yet not more real. An opening may be made in the body by a caustic as well as by an incision. God’s method in calling sinners may vary, but the effect is always the same.

Section V. The Properties of the Divine Call.

5. The properties of this call.

(1.) It is a sweet call. God calls in such a way that he allures; he does not force, but draws. The freedom of the will is not taken away, but its stubbornness is conquered128 (Ps 110:3): “Your people shall be willing in the day of Your power.” After this call there are no more disputes; the soul readily obeys God’s call. So when Christ called Zacchaeus, he joyfully welcomed him into his heart and his house.129

(2.) It is a holy call (2 Tim 1:9): “He has … called us to a holy calling.” This call of God calls men out of their sins; by it they are consecrated and set apart for God. The vessels of the tabernacle were taken from common use and set apart for a holy use. So those who are effectually called are separated from sin and consecrated to God’s service. The God whom we worship is holy, the work we are employed in is holy, and the place we hope to reach is holy; all this calls for holiness. A Christian’s heart is to be the presence chamber of the blessed Trinity; and shall not Holiness to the Lord be written on it? Believers are children of God the Father, members of God the Son, temples of God the Holy Spirit; and shall they not be holy? Holiness is the badge and uniform of God’s people (Isa 63:18): עם־קדשך, the people of your holiness. As chastity distinguishes a virtuous woman from a harlot, so holiness distinguishes the godly from the wicked. It is a holy calling. Let no man who lives in sin say he is called by God. Has God called you to be a swearer, to be a drunkard? No, and let not the merely moral person say he is effectually called. What is decency without holiness? It is only a dead body strewn with flowers. The king’s picture stamped on brass will not pass as money. The merely decent man looks as if he had the image of the King of heaven stamped on him, but he is no better than counterfeit metal, which God will not accept as genuine.

(3.) It is an irresistible call. When God calls a man by his grace, he cannot help coming. You+ may resist the minister’s call, but you+ cannot resist the Spirit’s call. The finger of the blessed Spirit can write on a heart of stone, as he once wrote his laws on tablets of stone. God’s words are verba creativa, creating words. When he said, “Let there be light,” there was light; and when he says, Let there be faith, it will be so. When God called Paul, he answered the call (Acts 26:19): “I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision”130. God rides out conquering in the chariot of his gospel. He makes the blind eye see and the stony heart bleed. If God will call a man, nothing will ponere obicem, or lie in the way to hinder it. Difficulties will be untied; the powers of hell will disband (Rom 9:19): “Who can resist His will?” God bends the iron sinew and breaks down the gates of bronze (Ps 107:16). When the Lord touches a man’s heart by his Spirit, all proud imaginations are brought down, and the royal fort of the will surrenders to God. I may allude to Ps 114:5: “What ailed you, O sea, that you fled, O Jordan, that you turned back?” The man who before was like a raging sea, foaming out wickedness, now suddenly flees back and trembles. He falls down like the jailer: “What must I do to be saved?” What ails you, O sea? What ails this man? The Lord has been effectually calling him; he has been working a work of grace, and now his stubborn heart is conquered by a sweet violence.

(4.) It is a high calling (Phil 3:14): “I press on toward the goal to win the prize of God’s high calling.” It is a high calling, first, because we are called to high exercises of religion: to die to sin, to be crucified to the world, to live by faith, to have fellowship with the Father (1 John 1:3). This is a high calling; here is a work too high for men in a state of nature to perform. Second, it is a high calling because we are called to high privileges: to justification and adoption, to be made co-heirs with Christ131. He who is effectually called is higher than the princes of the earth.

(5.) It is a gracious call; it is the fruit and product of free grace. God calls some and not others: one taken, and the other left. One is called who has a rougher, gloomier disposition, while another of sharper gifts and a sweeter temperament is rejected. Here is free grace! The poor are made rich in faith, and inherit the kingdom (Jas 2:5), while the nobles and great ones of the world are for the most part reprobated (1 Cor 1:26): “Not many of noble birth are called.” What is this but free and rich grace? Matt 11:26: “Yes, Father, for this was well-pleasing in Your sight.” In the same sermon one is effectually wrought on, and another is no more moved than a dead man by the sound of music. One hears the Spirit’s voice in the word; another does not hear it. One is softened and moistened with the influences of heaven; another, like Gideon’s dry fleece, has no dew on him. Behold here distinguishing grace! The same affliction converts one and hardens another. To the one, affliction is like the bruising of spices, which give out a fragrant smell. To the other, it is like the pounding of weeds in a mortar, which smell worse. Where does this come from but from the εὐδοκία, the free grace of God? It is a gracious calling; it is all enameled and interwoven with free grace. Si cogitare coeperis O anima mea, quot, & quales sint qui hanc quae tibi data est gratiam consequi non potuerunt; audisti certe quod multae gentes pertransierunt, quae omnes sine cognitione Dei in interitum sempiternum dilapsae sunt omnibus illis redemptor tuus te praetulit, gratiamque ejus largitus est; & quare hoc? Nullam praeter salvatoris Charitatem, invenire poteris Causam; elegit te in omnibus, assumpsit te ex omnibus, amavit te pre omnibus, ut memoriale ejus semper esset apud te132 [If you begin to think, O my soul, how many there are, and of what kind, who have not been able to obtain this grace that has been given to you: you have surely heard that many nations have passed away, all of which have fallen into everlasting ruin without the knowledge of God. Your Redeemer has preferred you to all of them and has given you his grace. And why this? You will find no cause except the love of the Savior. He chose you among all, took you out of all, loved you above all, so that the remembrance of him might always be with you].

(6.) It is a glorious call (1 Pet 5:10): “who has called us to His eternal glory.” We are called to the glorious enjoyment of the ever-blessed God. It is as if a man were called out of a prison to sit on a throne. Quintus Curtius writes of one who was digging in his garden when he was called to be king. So God calls us to glory and virtue (2 Pet 1:3): first to virtue, then to glory. At Athens there were two temples, the temple of virtue and the temple of honor, and no man could go into the temple of honor except through the temple of virtue. So God calls us first to virtue and then to glory. What is glory among men, which most people hunt after so, but a feather blown in the air? What is it compared with the weight of glory? Is there not great reason why we should follow God’s call? He calls us to promotion; can there be any loss or harm in this? God would have us part with nothing for him except what will damn us if we keep it. He has no design on us but to make us happy. He calls us to salvation; he calls us to a kingdom. Oh, how we should then, with Bartimaeus, throw off our ragged coat of sin and follow Christ when he calls!

(7.) It is a rare call. Only a few are savingly called (Matt 22:14): “Few are chosen.” Few, not taken all together, but by comparison. The word ἐκκαλεῖν, to call, signifies to choose some out from among others. Many have the light brought to them, but few have their eyes anointed to see that light (Rev 3:4): “You do have ὀλίγα ὀνόματα, a few names in Sardis who have not soiled their garments.” The devil has the vintage; God has only a few gleanings. How many millions sit in the region of darkness! And in those climates where the Sun of righteousness does shine, there are many who receive the light of the truth, but not the love of it. There are many formalists, but few believers. There is something that looks like faith which is not faith. The Cyprian diamond (says Pliny) sparkles like the true diamond, but it is not of the right kind; it will break under the hammer. So the hypocrite’s faith will break under the hammer of persecution. Only a few are truly called. Precious stones are few compared with the number of pebbles. Most men shape their religion to the fashion of the times; they are for the music and the idol (Dan 3:7). Serious thought about this would make us work out our salvation with fear, and labor to be among those few whom God has brought into a state of grace.

(8.) It is an unchangeable call (Rom 11:29): “God’s gifts and His call are χαρίσματα ἀμεταμέλητα, without repentance”; that is (as a learned writer says), those gifts that flow from election133. When God calls a man, he does not repent of it. God does not do as many friends do, love one day and hate the next; or as princes do, who make their subjects favorites and then throw them into prison. This is the blessedness of a saint: his condition admits of no change. God’s call is founded on his decree, and his decree is unchangeable. Acts of grace cannot be reversed. God blots out his people’s sins, but not their names. Let the world ring its changes every hour; a believer’s condition is fixed and unalterable.

Section VI. Showing the End of Effectual Calling.

6. The end of our heavenly calling is the honor of the most high God (Eph 1:12): “that we … would be for the praise of His glory.” He who is in the state of nature is no more fit to honor God than a beast is to perform acts of reason. A man before conversion continually brings dishonor on God. Black vapors rise out of fens and marshy ground and cloud and darken the sun. So black vapors of sin rise out of the natural man’s heart and cast a cloud on God’s glory. The sinner is well versed in treason, but understands nothing of loyalty to the King of heaven. Yes, but there are some on whom the lot of free grace falls. These will be taken like jewels from among the rubbish and be effectually called, so that they may lift up God’s name and honor in the world. The Lord will have some in every age who will oppose the corruptions of the times, bear witness to his truths, and turn sinners from the error of their ways. He will have his mighty men, as King David had. Those who have been monuments of God’s mercy will be trumpets of his praise.

125. Nihil durius servitute. [Nothing is harder than slavery.] Cicero.

126. Nisi spiritus adsit cordi audientis, inanis est labor docentis. [Unless the Spirit is present in the heart of the hearer, the labor of the teacher is in vain.]

127. Rev 3:7.

128. Actio haec non fit coactio; Deus non torquet, sed trahit. [This action is not compulsion; God does not wrench, but draws.]

129. μὴ βουλομένους οὐ βιάζεται ὁ θεὸς ἀλλὰ ἕλκει. [God does not force the unwilling, but draws them.]

130. Παῦλος μὲν ἀκούσας φωνῆς, εὐθέως ὑπήκουσε, καὶ πολλὴν ἐπεδείξατο τὴν μεταβολήν. [Paul, when he heard the voice, obeyed at once and showed a great change.] Chrysostom.

131. Rom 8:17 συγκληρονόμοι Aeternae vitae & gloriae participes; aperiuntur, hic nobis limpidissimi fontes, etc. [Sharers of eternal life and glory; here the clearest springs are opened to us.] Beza.

132. Augustine.

133. Willet.

Chapter XII

Two inferences drawn from the proposition.

1. It shows us the necessity of effectual calling. Without it there is no going to heaven. We must be made fit for the inheritance (Col 1:12). As God makes heaven fit for us, so he makes us fit for heaven. And what gives this fitness and suitability but effectual calling? A man who remains in the filth and rubbish of nature is no more fit for heaven than a dead man is fit to inherit. The high calling is not a thing optional or left to our choice; it is as necessary as salvation. Yet, alas, how this one needful thing is neglected! Most men, like the people of Israel, wander up and down to gather straw, but pay no attention to evidences of their effectual calling.

2. Take notice what a mighty power God puts forth in calling sinners134! God so calls that he draws (John 6:44). Conversion is called a resurrection (Rev 20:6): “Blessed … are those who share in the first resurrection!” That is a rising from sin to grace. A man can no more convert himself than a dead man can raise himself. It is called a creation (Col 3:10). To create is above the power of nature.

But the Arminians say that the will is not dead but asleep. God by a moral persuasion only wakes us, they say, and then the will can obey God’s call and move of itself to its own conversion135.

To this I answer: every man is bound in fetters by sin (Acts 8:23)136: “I see that you are … in the bond of iniquity.” If you use arguments with a man who is in fetters and persuade him to walk, is that enough? His fetters must be knocked off and he must be set free before he can walk. So it is with every natural man: he is fettered with corruption. Now the Lord by converting grace must file off his fetters, and indeed give him legs to run as well, or he can never obtain salvation.

134. 2 Branch.

135. Objection.

136. Answer.

Chapter XIII

Exhorting to the heavenly calling.

2. Labor to make it clear to your+ own souls that you+ are savingly called (2 Pet 1:10): “Strive to make your+ calling … sure.” This is the great business of our lives: to get sound evidence of our effectual calling. Do not rest content with outward privileges. Do not cry, as the Jews did, “The temple of the Lord.” Do not rest in baptism; what is it to have the water and lack the Spirit? Do not be content that you+ were born within the sound of Aaron’s bells, that Christ has been preached to you+. Do not satisfy yourselves+ with an empty profession. All this may be so, and yet you+ are no better than blazing comets. But labor to make it evident to your+ souls that you+ are called by God. Do not be Athenians, asking for news: What is the state and complexion of the times? What will be the effects of such an eclipse? What changes are likely to happen in such a year? What is all this if you+ are not effectually called? What if the times should take on a fairer look? What does it matter if glory dwells in our land, if grace does not dwell in our hearts?137 O my brothers, when things are dark outside, let all be clear within. “Strive to make your+ calling … sure.” It is both possible and likely; God does not fail those who seek him. Do not let this great business hang unfinished any longer. If there were a dispute about your+ land, you+ would use every means to clear your+ title. And is salvation nothing? Will you+ not clear your+ title here? Consider how sad your+ case is if you+ are not effectually called.

(1.) You+ are strangers to God. The prodigal went into a far country (Luke 15:13), to show that every sinner before conversion is far off from God (Eph 2:12): “At that time you+ were separate from Christ, … strangers to the covenants of the promise.” Men dying in their sins have no more right to the promises than strangers have to the privileges of freeborn citizens. If you+ are strangers, what word can you+ expect from God but this: “I do not know you+”?

(2.) If you+ are not effectually called, you+ are enemies (Col 1:21): “alienated from God and … enemies in your+ minds.” There is nothing in the Bible you+ can lay claim to but the threats. You+ are heirs to all the plagues written in the book of God. Though you+ may resist the commands of the law, you+ cannot escape the curses of the law. Let those who are enemies to God read their doom in Luke 19:27: “These enemies of mine who were unwilling for me to rule over them, bring them here and slay them in front of me.” Oh, then, how closely it concerns you+ to make your+ calling sure! How miserable and damnable your+ condition will be if death calls you+ before the Spirit calls you+!

Question 1. But is there any hope of my being called? I have been a great sinner.

Answer. Great sinners have been called. Paul was as bloody a persecutor as Domitian or Julian ever was, yet he was called138. Some of the Jews who had a hand in crucifying Christ were called. God loves to display the flag of free grace to sinners. So do not be discouraged. You see a golden cord let down from heaven for poor trembling souls to lay hold of.

Signs of Effectual Calling

Question 2. But how shall I know that I am effectually called?

Answer. 1. He who is savingly called is called out of himself, not only out of sinful self but out of righteous self. He renounces trust in his duties and moral endowments (Phil 3:9): “not having my own righteousness.” He whose heart God has touched by his Spirit lays down the idol of self-righteousness at Christ’s feet for him to tread on. He practices morality and duties of godliness, but he does not trust in them. Noah’s dove made use of her wings to fly, but trusted in the ark for safety. It is an excellent thing when a man is called out of himself. This self-renunciation is (as Augustine says) primus ad fidem aditus, the first step to saving faith.

2. He who is effectually called has a visible change worked in him: not a change of the faculties, but of the qualities. He is altered from what he was before. His body is the same, but not his mind. He has a different spirit139 he is alter idem [another, and yet the same]. Paul was so changed after his conversion that people did not know him (Acts 9:21). Oh, what a transformation grace makes! 1 Cor 6:11: “And that is what some of you+ were. But you+ were … sanctified, you+ were justified”140. Grace is the true Verticordia; it turns the heart. In effectual calling a threefold change is worked.

(1.) A change is worked in the understanding. Before, there was ignorance; “darkness was over the surface of the deep.” But now there is light (Eph 5:8): “Now you+ are light in the Lord.” The first work God made was light, and so it is in the new creation. He who is savingly called says with that man in the gospel (John 9:25), “I was blind, but now I see!” He sees an evil in sin, and an excellence in the ways of God, such as he never saw before. Indeed, this light that the blessed Spirit brings may well be called θαυμαστὸν φῶς, a marvelous light (1 Pet 2:9): “to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you+ … into His marvelous light”141. It is a marvelous light in six respects. (1) Because it is strangely conveyed. It does not come from the heavenly spheres, where the planets are, but from the Sun of righteousness. (2) It is marvelous in its effect. This light does what no other light can: it makes a man see that he is blind. (3) It is a marvelous light because it is more penetrating. Other light may shine on the face; this light shines on the heart and enlightens the conscience (2 Cor 4:6). (4) It is a marvelous light because it sets those who have it marveling. They marvel at themselves, how they could be content so long without it. They marvel that their eyes should be opened and not others’. They marvel that, though they hated and opposed this light, it should still shine in the sky of their souls. This is what the saints will stand wondering at for all eternity. (5) It is a marvelous light because it has more power than any other. It not only enlightens, but enlivens; it makes alive those who were dead in their trespasses and sins. That is why it is so fittingly called lumen vitae, the light of life (John 8:12). (6) It is a marvelous light because it is the beginning of the everlasting light. The light of grace is the morning star that ushers in the sunlight of glory.

Now then, Christian, can you say that this marvelous light of the Spirit has dawned on you? When you were wrapped in ignorance and knew neither God nor yourself, suddenly a light from heaven shone around you. This is one part of the blessed change that is worked in effectual calling.

(2.) A change is worked in the will (Rom 7:18): “I have the will to do what is good.” The will, which before opposed Christ, now embraces him. The will, which was an iron sinew, is now like melting wax; it readily receives the stamp and impression of the Holy Spirit. The will, like the primum mobile [the first mover], moves heavenward and carries all the spheres of the affections along with it. The regenerate will answers every call of God as the echo answers the voice (Acts 9:6): “Lord, what do You want me to do?” The will now becomes a volunteer; it enlists under the Captain of salvation142. Oh, what a happy change is worked here! Before, the will kept Christ out; now it keeps sin out.

(3.) There is a change in the conduct. He who is called by God walks directly contrary to the way he walked before. Before, he walked in envy and malice; now he walks in love. Before, he walked in pride; now in humility. The current is carried quite another way (Acts 23:1): “I have conducted myself before God in all good conscience.” As in the heart there is a new birth, so in the life there is a new edition. So we see what a mighty change is worked in those who are called by God.

How far from this effectual call are those who have never had any change! They are the same as they were forty or fifty years ago, as proud and carnal as ever. They have seen many changes in the times, but they have had no change in their hearts. Let men not think to go to heaven per saltum, to leap out of the harlot’s lap into Abraham’s bosom. Either they must have a gracious change while they live, or a cursed change when they die.

3. He who is called by God values this call as the highest blessing. A king whom God has called by his grace counts it more that he is called to be a saint than that he is called to be a king. He values his high calling above his high birth. Theodosius thought it a greater honor to be a Christian than to be an emperor. A carnal person can no more value spiritual blessings than a child can value a cluster of diamonds. He prefers his worldly grandeur, his ease, his plenty, his titles of honor, to conversion. He would rather be called Duke than Saint; it is a sign that he is a stranger to effectual calling. He who is enlightened by the Spirit counts holiness his best coat of arms, and looks on his effectual calling as his promotion. When he has taken this degree, he is a candidate for heaven.

4. He who is effectually called is called out of the world. It is a heavenly calling (Heb 3:1). He who is called by God sets his mind on things of a heavenly kind. He is in the world, but not of the world. Naturalists say of precious stones that though they have their matter from the earth, their sparkling luster comes from the influence of the heavens. So it is with a godly man: though his body is from the earth, the sparkle of his affections is from heaven. His heart is drawn up into the upper region, as high as Christ. He casts off not only every wicked work but every earthly weight. He is not a worm but an eagle.

5. Another sign of our effectual calling is diligence in our ordinary calling. Some boast of their high calling, but they lie idle at anchor. Religion does not sign warrants for idleness. Christians must not be like Leviathan, which was made to frolic in the sea (Ps 104:26). Idleness is balneum diaboli, the devil’s bath; a lazy person becomes a prey to every temptation. Grace, while it cures the heart, does not make the hand lame. He who is called by God works at his trade, just as he works for heaven143. Now if on searching you+ can find that you+ are effectually called, I have three exhortations for you+.

Chapter XIV

Three exhortations to those who are called.

Wonder at Free Grace

1. Wonder at God’s free grace in calling you+, and adore it. That God should leap over so many, that he should pass by the wise and noble, and that the lot of free grace should fall on you+! That he should take you+ out of a state of slavery, from grinding at the devil’s mill, and set you+ above the princes of the earth, and call you+ to inherit the throne of glory! Fall on your+ knees; break out into a thankful triumph of praise. Let your+ hearts be ten-stringed instruments to sound out the memory of God’s mercy. No one is so deep in debt to free grace as you+, and no one should climb so high on the pinnacle of thanksgiving. Say with the sweet singer (Ps 145:2): “I will exalt You, my God and King; … Every day I will bless You, and I will praise Your name forever and ever.” Those who are patterns of mercy should be trumpets of praise. Oh, long to be in heaven, where your+ thanksgivings will be purer and will be raised a note higher.

Pity Those Who Are Uncalled

2. Pity those who are not yet called. Sinners in scarlet are objects not of envy but of pity. They are under the power of Satan (Acts 26:18). Every day they walk along the edge of the bottomless pit; and what if death should give them a push? Oh, pity unconverted sinners. If you+ pity an ox or a donkey that goes astray, will you+ not pity a soul going astray from God, who has lost his way and his wits and is on the brink of damnation?

Indeed, do not only pity sinners, but pray for them. Though they curse, you+ pray. You+ would pray for people who are out of their minds, and sinners are out of their minds (Luke 15:17): “He came to himself.” It seems the prodigal was not himself before his conversion. Wicked men are going to execution. Sin is the noose that strangles them, death turns them off the ladder, and hell is their burial place. And will you+ not pray for them when you+ see them in such danger?

Walk Worthy of Your High Calling

3. You+ who are effectually called, honor your+ high calling (Eph 4:1): “I urge you+ to walk in a manner worthy144 of the calling you+ have received.” Christians must keep a fitting decorum; they must observe τὸ πρέπον, what is becoming145. This is timely advice, when many who profess to be called by God bring a blemish on religion by their loose and careless walk, so that the ways of God are spoken evil of. It is a saying of Salvian: what do pagans say when they see Christians live scandalously? “Surely Christ taught them no better.” Will you+ reproach Christ and make him suffer again by abusing your+ heavenly calling146? It is one of the saddest sights to see a man lift up his hands in prayer and with those hands oppress; to hear the same tongue praise God and at another time lie and slander; to hear a man profess God in words and deny him in works. Oh, how unworthy this is! Yours+ is a holy calling, and will you+ be unholy? Do not think you+ may take liberties as others do. The Nazirite who had a vow on him separated himself to God and promised abstinence. Though others drank wine, it was not fitting for the Nazirite to do so. So though others are loose and vain, it is not fitting for those who are set apart for God by effectual calling. Shall not flowers smell sweeter than weeds? You+ must be λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν, a special people (1 Pet 2:9): special not only in dignity but in conduct. Scorn things that are base and foreign to the gospel. Scipio refused the embraces of a harlot because he was general of an army. Abhor every impulse to sin, because it will disgrace your+ high calling.

Question. What is it to walk worthy of our heavenly calling?

Answer. 1. It is to walk by rule, when we tread with an even foot and walk according to the rules and principles of the word. A true saint is for canonical obedience; he follows the canon of Scripture, as the Greek word is (Gal 6:16): “all who walk by this canon”147. When we leave men’s inventions and cling to God’s ordinances; when we walk after the word as Israel walked after the pillar of fire: this is walking worthy of our heavenly calling.

(2.) To walk worthy of our calling is to walk apart from the crowd (Gen 7:1): Noah was upright in his generation. When others walked with the devil, Noah walked with God. We are forbidden to run with the multitude (Exod 23:2). Though in secular matters it is not commendable to be singular, in religion it is good to be singular. Melanchthon was the glory of the age he lived in. Athanasius was singularly holy; he stood up for God when the stream of the times ran another way. It is better to be a pattern of holiness than a partner in wickedness. It is better to go to heaven with a few than to hell in the crowd. We must walk directly opposite to the men of the world, as the Antipodes are to us.

(3.) To walk worthy of our calling is to walk cheerfully (Phil 4:4): “Rejoice in the Lord always.” Too much drooping of spirit disgraces our high calling, and makes others suspect the godly life to be sour and melancholy. Of all temperaments, Christ loves the cheerful. Caussin in his Hieroglyphics speaks of a dove whose wings were perfumed with sweet ointments, and so drew the other doves after her. Cheerfulness is a perfume to draw others to godliness. Religion does not banish all mirth. As there is a seriousness without sourness, so there is a cheerfulness without levity. When the prodigal was converted, “they began to celebrate” (Luke 15:24). Who should be cheerful if not the people of God? No sooner are they born of the Spirit148 than they are heirs to a crown. God is their portion and heaven is their mansion, and shall they not rejoice?

(4.) To walk worthy of our calling is to walk wisely. Walking wisely implies three things.

[1.] To walk carefully (Eccl 2:14): “The wise man has eyes in his head.” Others watch for our stumbling, and so we need to look to our footing. We must beware not only of scandals but of improprieties, in case by our indiscretion we open the mouths of others with a fresh cry against religion. If our godliness will not convert men, our prudence may silence them.

[2.] To walk courteously. The spirit of the gospel is full of sweetness and kindness (1 Pet 3:8): “Be courteous,” φιλόφρονες. Beware of a gloomy, haughty manner. Religion does not take away good manners, but refines them (Gen 23:7): “Abraham rose and bowed down before the people of the land, the Hittites.” Though they were of a heathen race, Abraham showed them civil respect. Paul had a friendly temperament (1 Cor 9:20): “I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some.” In lesser matters the apostle gave way to others, so that by his obliging conduct he might win them over and catch them by a holy guile.

[3.] To walk with greatness of spirit. Though we must be humble, we must not be base. It is unworthy to prostitute ourselves to the lusts of men. What is sinfully imposed ought to be zealously opposed. Conscience is God’s diocese, where no one has a right to visit but he who is the Bishop of our souls (1 Pet 2:25). We must not be like hot iron, which can be beaten into any shape. A brave-spirited Christian will rather die than allow the virginity of his conscience to be defiled by superstition. Here the serpent and the dove are united, shrewdness and innocence. This prudent walking fits our high calling and does much to adorn the gospel of Christ.

(5.) To walk worthy of our calling is to walk with influence on others: to do good to others, and to be rich in acts of mercy (Heb 13:16).149 Good works honor religion. As Mary poured the ointment on Christ, so by good works we pour sweet ointment on the head of the gospel and make it give out a fragrant smell. Though good works are not causes of salvation, they are evidences of it. When with our Savior we go about doing good, and send out the refreshing influences of our generosity, then we walk worthy of our high calling.

(3.) Lastly,150 here is matter of comfort for you+ who are effectually called. God has made his rich grace great toward you+. You+ are called to great honor: to be partners with the angels and co-heirs with Christ. This should revive you+ in the worst of times. Let men reproach you+ and call you+ names; set God’s calling of you+ against man’s miscalling. Let men persecute you+ to death; they only give you+ a passport and send you+ to heaven sooner. How this may cure the trembling of the heart! What though the sea roars, though the earth is unquiet, though the stars are shaken out of their places? You+ need not fear. You+ are called, and so you+ are sure to be crowned.

God’s Eternal Purpose

Chapter XV

Concerning God’s purpose.

3. The third and last thing in the text, which I will only glance at briefly, is the ground and origin of our effectual calling, in these words: κατὰ πρόθεσιν, “according to His purpose.” Anselm renders it according to his good will151. Peter Martyr reads it κατὰ γνώμην, according to his decree, and Beza interprets it the same way. This purpose, or decree, of God is the fountainhead of all our spiritual blessings152. It is the causa προηγουμένη, the moving cause of our calling, justification, and glorification. It is the highest link in the golden chain of salvation. Why is one man called and not another? It is from the eternal purpose of God. God’s decree gives the casting vote in man’s salvation.

151. Signif. aeternum Dei beneplacitum. [It signifies the eternal good pleasure of God.] Anselm.

152. πρόθεσις est decretum Dei, ab aeterno sanctum, ex mera ipsius non scrutanda sed adoranda voluntate. [Πρόθεσις is the decree of God, ordained from eternity out of his sheer will, which is not to be searched into but adored.] Beza

Chapter XVI

Showing that all must be traced back to God’s purpose.

Let us ascribe the whole work of grace to the good pleasure of God’s will153. God did not choose us because we were worthy, but by choosing us he makes us worthy. Proud men are apt to claim and take too much to themselves, as if they shared the work with God. While many cry out against sacrilege against the church, they are meanwhile guilty of a far greater sacrilege: they rob God of his glory when they set out to put the crown of salvation on their own head. But we must trace everything back to God’s purpose. The signs of salvation are in the saints, but the cause of salvation is in God. If it is God’s purpose that saves, then:

1. It is not free will. The Pelagians are strenuous defenders of free will. They tell us that a man has an inborn power for his own conversion. But this text refutes it: our calling is according to God’s purpose. The Scripture pulls up the weed of free will by the roots (Rom 9:16): “It does not depend on man’s will.” Everything depends on the πρόθεσις, the purpose of God. When the prisoner is condemned at the bar, there is no saving him unless the King has a purpose to save him. God’s purpose is his royal prerogative.

2. If it is God’s purpose that saves, then it is not merit. Bellarmine holds that good works atone for sin and merit glory. No, the text says we are called according to God’s purpose; and there is a parallel Scripture, 2 Tim 1:9: “He has saved us and called us …, not because of our works, but by His own purpose and grace.” There is no such thing as merit. Our best works have in them both defect and infection, and so they are only splendida peccata, glittering sins. So if we are called and justified, it is God’s purpose that brings it about.

Objection. But the papists cite this Scripture for merit, 2 Tim 4:8: “From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day.” This is the force of their argument: if God in justice rewards our works, then they merit salvation.

Response. To this I answer, first, that God gives a reward as a just Judge, not to the worthiness of our works, but to the worthiness of Christ. Second, God as a just Judge rewards us, not because we have deserved it, but because he has promised it154; God has two courts, a court of mercy and a court of justice. The Lord condemns in the court of justice those works which he crowns in the court of mercy. So what carries the main stroke in our salvation is the πρόθεσις, the purpose of God.

3. If the purpose of God is the fountainhead of happiness, then we are not saved for faith foreseen. It is absurd to think that anything in us could have the least influence on our election155. The Arminians say that God foresaw that such persons would believe, and therefore chose them; and so they would make the business of salvation depend on something in us. But God does not choose us for faith, but to faith (Eph 1:4): “He chose us … to be holy”: not because we would be holy, but so that we might be holy. We are elected to holiness, not for it156. What could God foresee in us but pollution and rebellion? If any man is saved, it is κατὰ πρόθεσιν, according to God’s purpose.

Question. How shall we know that God has a purpose to save us?

Answer. By being effectually called. 2 Pet 1:10: “Strive to make your+ calling and election sure.” We make our election sure by making our calling sure. 2 Thess 2:13: “God has chosen you+ … to be saved by the sanctification of the Spirit.” By the stream we come at last to the fountain. If we find the stream of sanctification running in our souls, we may by this come to the fountainhead of election. When a man’s eyes are so weak that he cannot look up to the sky, he may still know the moon is there by seeing it shine on the water. So though I do not look up into the secret of God’s purpose, I may know I am elected by the shining of sanctifying grace in my soul. Whoever finds the word of God transcribed and copied out into his heart may conclude beyond denial that he is elected.157

The Saints’ Comforts Built upon This Impregnable Rock

Use. 2. Here is a sovereign elixir, an unspeakable comfort for those who are the called of God: their salvation rests on God’s purpose (2 Tim 2:19): “God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are His.’” Our graces are imperfect; our comforts ebb and flow; but God’s firm foundation stands. Those who are built on this rock of God’s eternal purpose need not fear falling away. Neither the power of man nor the violence of temptation will ever be able to overturn them.
